articles.title: In 1934, a gun club opened on 9.5 acres beside San Franciscoâs Lake Merced; 81 years later it closed, contaminated soil was cleaned up and the lakeside land is now being opened for public recreation
articles.summary: US News: San Francisco city officials have opened a search for private partners to redevelop a 9.5-acre lakeside property that was used as a private shooting r.
articles.body: San Francisco city officials have opened a search for private partners to redevelop a 9.5-acre lakeside property that was used as a private shooting range for more than 80 years. The move marks the final stage of a major environmental transformation along the western shore of Lake Merced. The property at 520 John Muir Drive was home to the Pacific Rod and Gun Club from 1934 until it permanently closed in 2015. After years of environmental cleanup, the city is now seeking proposals to turn the site into a public park and recreation centre.Decades of shooting leave toxic legacyThe Pacific Rod and Gun Club opened on the shores of Lake Merced in 1934, with skeet, trap and rifle ranges for local shooters. During more than 80 years of operation, shooting left large amounts of lead pellets and debris from petroleum-based clay targets in the soil and along the lake shore. When the club's lease ended in 2015, city officials closed the facility and began dealing with the pollution. The property is one of the largest areas of flat waterfront land around Lake Merced outside the nearby Harding Park Golf Course. According to announcements from the San Francisco Recreation and Park Department, the San Francisco Public Utilities Commission managed a large, multi-stage environmental cleanup. Workers removed polluted soil and heavy metals, demolished old shooting structures and made the land safe again. The final stage of the cleanup was completed in 2025, allowing the public to safely use the property.City seeks ideas for a new waterfrontWith the cleanup complete, the city has issued a formal Request for Proposals (RFP) for the site, which is known as Lake Merced West. Under city rules, the land will remain publicly owned. Any future development must focus on public access, outdoor recreation and community facilities. In a public announcement released through the San Francisco Recreation and Park Department, District 7 Supervisor Myrna Melgar described the opportunity to create a new destination along the lake. "Lake Merced is one of San Francisco's most important natural resources, and it is also a beloved place for recreation and discovery. I'm excited to see the creativity and imagination that come forward in response to this RFP," said District 7 Supervisor Myrna Melgar. "This is a rare opportunity to reimagine a significant piece of our public waterfront, and I look forward to seeing ideas that expand access, celebrate the lake's natural setting and create new ways for San Franciscans to enjoy this incredible resource."Plans for a new lakeside destinationThe city's planning framework lists several possible uses for the 9.5-acre property. Officials are seeking ideas that could include:Water access: A new boathouse, floating dock and soft-launch area for rowers, kayakers and stand-up paddleboarders.Community facilities: Outdoor dining areas, cafes, multi-sport courts and a community recreation building.Outdoor recreation: Walking trails, areas for birdwatching, adventure rope courses and children's play spaces.The Recreation and Park Department said the entire property does not have to be developed by one organisation. The city could divide the site between several non-profit groups or commercial operators, creating a larger mix of recreational facilities. The redevelopment would bring nearly a century of restricted waterfront land back into public use. Once a private shooting range, the former Pacific Rod and Gun Club property is now set to become part of San Francisco's wider public park and recreation network.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A Tennessee company is breaking down retired wind turbine blades instead of sending them to landfills, recovering glass fibre at 99.9% purity that can be reused in concrete, car panels and 3D-printing filament
articles.summary: US News: Retired wind turbine blades are becoming a growing waste challenge as older turbines reach the end of their operating lives, but a Tennessee company i.
articles.body: Retired wind turbine blades are becoming a growing waste challenge as older turbines reach the end of their operating lives, but a Tennessee company is developing a way to recover valuable material from them instead of sending the blades to landfill. Carbon Rivers, a Knoxville-based advanced materials company, uses a heat-based process to separate glass fibre from the polymers and resins that hold turbine blades together. The US Department of Energy has reported that the company achieved 99.9% purity in recovered glass fibre, creating the possibility of using the material again in products such as composite panels, construction materials and 3D-printing filament. The technology has received millions of dollars in federal support and research collaboration with the University of Tennessee, Knoxville. Rather than treating an old blade as waste, the process aims to turn its materials into feedstock for new manufacturing.How a Tennessee company is recycling retired wind turbine bladesCarbon Rivers is tackling one of the hardest parts of wind turbine recycling by targeting the composite material used in the blades. The US Department of Energy estimates that around 85% to 90% of a wind turbine's mass can already be recycled, with steel, copper and other materials having established recycling routes. The remaining fraction is much more difficult because turbine blades are made from fibre-reinforced composites, in which glass fibres are embedded in tough polymer resins. Those materials are designed to resist fatigue, weather and repeated mechanical stress, but the same durability makes them difficult to separate at the end of their service life. Carbon Rivers uses a process known as pyrolysis, which heats the composite in the absence of oxygen so that the organic resin and polymer components break down while the inorganic glass fibres remain. The recovered fibres can then be cleaned and processed for reuse. The approach is intended to preserve more of the material's value than simply grinding blades into waste or using them in low-value applications.The recycling process works by exploiting the different behaviour of organic and inorganic materials when exposed to intense heat. During pyrolysis, the polymer components of the blade decompose without oxygen, producing hydrocarbon products including syngas and pyrolysis oil. Carbon Rivers can recover these materials for energy-related uses while separating the glass fibre reinforcement from the composite. Once separated, the fibre can be cleaned and prepared for manufacturing applications. The US Department of Energy reported that Carbon Rivers achieved 99.9% recycled glass fibre purity, a level that could allow the recovered material to be used in applications that would otherwise require virgin fibreglass. Carbon Rivers describes its technology as Glass to Glass reclamation, with the aim of taking glass-fibre composites at the end of their useful life and returning the recovered fibre to manufacturing. The process has also been investigated for other composite waste streams, including materials from the automotive and marine industries, suggesting that the technology could eventually address a broader waste problem rather than being limited to wind turbine blades.The recovered material can be used in new productsThe biggest potential advantage of recovering the glass fibre is that it can be turned into useful manufacturing material rather than simply disposed of. DOE has identified applications including non-woven mats, continuous textile yarns, thermoplastic pellets, automotive sheet-moulding compounds and filament for 3D printing. Recovered glass fibre can also be incorporated into construction materials and potentially remelted or blended with virgin fibreglass for other uses. This creates the possibility of a more circular system in which the material from an old turbine blade becomes part of another product instead of ending up in a landfill. Carbon Rivers has also worked on applications beyond wind energy, including automotive, marine and structural composite materials. That matters because glass-fibre composites are used in many industries, creating a much larger potential market for recovered material. The technology could eventually allow manufacturers to use recycled glass fibre in products such as vehicle panels, building components and other composite products while reducing their dependence on newly manufactured fibreglass.Millions in government funding helped scale the technologyCarbon Rivers' technology has received substantial support from the US Department of Energy. DOE reported that the company received approximately $2.4 million through its Wind Energy Technologies Office and Small Business Technology Transfer programme beginning in 2019, with researchers at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, working with the company to scale up the recovery process. By 2022, DOE said Carbon Rivers had upcycled more than 100 tons of wind turbine blade material into products such as non-woven mats, thermoplastic pellets and 3D-printing filament. A later DOE report said the company had processed a few thousand metric tons and was working towards much greater processing capacity. In 2023, the company also received a $1.1 million Phase III award through DOE's wind-energy technology programme to further develop the recycling process and support the use of recovered glass fibre in new composite applications. DOE has described the work as an example of technology development moving from research towards commercialisation. The government support is particularly significant because recycling old blades requires not only a technically effective process but also enough capacity to handle large and irregular waste streams generated by the wind industry.Tennessee could help build a more circular wind industryCarbon Rivers is based in Knoxville, Tennessee, and its recycling work has been linked to plans for a larger facility in nearby Kingston. The original DOE announcement described plans for a facility at a historic site associated with the Manhattan Project and said it was expected to process thousands of wind turbine blades each year. Those original projections should not be treated as confirmation that the facility opened on schedule, but they illustrate the scale the company was targeting as it moved from pilot work towards commercial processing. The broader need is clear. DOE says most of a wind turbine can already be recycled, but composite blades remain a major challenge, and many retired blades still go to landfill because recycling capacity and economics remain limited. Carbon Rivers is one of several companies and research groups working to change that situation. Its process does not mean every old turbine blade can now be recycled cheaply or indefinitely, but recovering high-purity glass fibre creates another route for keeping valuable material in circulation. If the technology can be scaled economically, retired blades could become a source of manufacturing feedstock for construction, automotive products, 3D printing and potentially new wind turbine components, helping reduce the amount of composite waste sent to landfill as the wind industry continues to expand.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.body: Nepal parliament secretariat cleared PM Balendra Shah to wear his trademark dark sunglasses inside parliament on medical grounds after his office submitted a medical report, ending a row over whether such eyewear belonged in the House. Shah is scheduled to face lawmakers in a direct question-and-answer session on Wednesday, amid opposition criticism over his repeated absence from parliament.Shahâs rectangular black shades had long been part of his public image, accompanying the former rapper and Kathmandu mayor through his rise to Nepalâs top office. Ahead of Nepalâs March 5 elections, supporters dubbed the look âBalen dai ko chashmaâ, triggering a fashion craze among young voters. Similar black rectangular frames sold out at several Kathmandu shops and online stores as demand surged, with retailers marketing lookalikes. articles.title: Emmanuel Nchimbi: Tanzania's vice-president announces resignation in unprecedented move
articles.summary: Emmanuel Nchimbi is the first vice-president to quit since independence six decades ago.
articles.body:
Tanzania's Vice-President Emmanuel Nchimbi has announced he is resigning weeks after it was reported that he had fallen out with President Samia Suluhu Hassan.

The 54-year-old shared his brief resignation letter on his Instagram account, saying he wanted to respect the president's wishes. Sources in his office and the presidency confirmed the move.

Nchimbi said he would retire from public life at the end of next week - less than 10 months after being sworn in and making him the first vice-president to step down in the history of the East African nation.

He was Samia's running mate in last October's disputed presidential election, which saw hundreds killed in post-poll unrest.

The pair were sworn in last November after winning 98% of the vote.

Violent protests in the awake of voting led to the deaths of at least 500 people, according to an official enquiry .

Opposition parties and human rights groups accused the security forces of unleashing a brutal crackdown on anti-government protesters.

"I have become convinced, without doubt, that the president wants changes, and I have therefore decided to fulfil my promise," Nchimbi wrote in his resignation letter referring to the pledge he had made to Samia that he would go if she wanted another deputy.

He thanked the president and the ruling Chama Cha Mapinduzi (CCM) party for the trust they had placed in him, and to Tanzanians for their support during his time in public service.

Nchimbi said he was leaving office in accordance with the country's constitution and would continue to be a "good citizen of Tanzania".

The vice-president has made some controversial remarks in recent weeks - which may point to the possible fallout with President Samia.

Last month, he urged Tanzanians to "fight for a new constitution", arguing that there was an opportunity to secure one before 2030.

He also linked a new constitution to ways of addressing injustice, strengthening human rights, good governance and democracy.

Nchimbi previously served as secretary-general of CCM. He also held several senior positions in government, including both minister of information and home affairs, before becoming Tanzania's ambassador to Brazil and later Egypt.

articles.title: Federal judge slaps down Ghislaine Maxwell petition for new trial as ‘rambling,’ ‘meritless’
articles.summary: Judge Paul Engelmayer called Ghislaine Maxwell's post-conviction challenge "meritless" and "frivolous," finding trial evidence against her "overwhelming."
articles.body: A federal judge rejected Ghislaine Maxwell’s latest effort to overturn her conviction, blasting her petition as "lengthy and rambling" and finding her claims "all meritless" and "all or almost all" frivolous. U.S. District Judge Paul A. Engelmayer denied Maxwell’s post-conviction challenge in an opinion filed Monday in the Southern District of New York and made public Tuesday, writing that the evidence against the convicted Jeffrey Epstein associate at trial was "overwhelming." Maxwell, representing herself, had moved to vacate her conviction and 20-year prison sentence, alleging that her constitutional rights were violated at trial and sentencing. TODD BLANCHE SAYS 'NO CLOSED INVESTIGATIONS' IN EPSTEIN CASE, VOWS DOJ WILL PURSUE NEW SUSPECTS Engelmayer said the vast majority of her arguments were procedurally barred because she either raised and lost them on direct appeal or could have raised them earlier but did not. The judge also shot down Maxwell’s reliance on material released under the Epstein Files Transparency Act, finding that the purported new evidence did not support her claims. The supposedly "new" evidence was largely irrelevant to  Maxwell 's case, the judge said. FORMER ATTORNEY GENERAL PAM BONDI HAILS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION'S 'JUSTICE AND TRANSPARENCY' ON EPSTEIN FILES "To the extent it is relevant, far from exculpating her, it incriminates her or reinforces the correctness of the legal rulings Maxwell challenges," Engelmayer wrote. "The Court accordingly denies Maxwell’s petition," he concluded. articles.title: 'Where to kill Barron Trump?' Iranian video targets US prez's son; Secret Service probes footage
articles.summary: US News: The US Secret Service has acknowledged being aware of a video being broadcast by Iranian state media that appeared to threaten the life of Barron Trum.
articles.body: The US Secret Service has acknowledged being aware of a video being broadcast by Iranian state media that appeared to threaten the life of Barron Trump. They have stated that they are investigating the footage as a potential threat to a protected person.The nearly three-minute video, aired over the weekend by Iranâs state broadcaster IRIB, opened with an English-language graphic asking, âWhere to kill Barron Trump?â It featured images and references to places where the 20-year-old is publicly known to spend time, including New Yorkâs Trump Tower and locations associated with his studies at New York University.It further states that it uncovered Barronâs accounts for video games and Discord, as well as those of his classmates, naming two of them.The video ended with a reference to a reported $10 million reward and a warning directed at Barron. The footage was also circulated by Iranian media outlets and affiliated social media accounts.A Secret Service spokesperson told CNN that the agency was aware of the video and investigates âanything that can be perceived as a threatâ toward people under its protection. The agency declined to provide further details, citing operational security and the sensitivity of protective intelligence.The video appears to be part of a wider campaign of threats against the Trump family in Iranian hardline media following the death of former Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei during the US-Israeli war with Iran.A US federal law enforcement source told CNN that previous videos had also targeted President Trump and other members of his family, sometimes including references to their movements and locations.Threats against Trump have intensified since the conflict began. Trump has previously said he was aware of Iranian efforts to target him, while US officials have taken additional precautions around his travel and security.Iranian media had earlier circulated similar material targeting First Lady Melania Trump, including content purporting to identify places she visits and details about her movements.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Bluefaceâs livestream takes shocking turn as police detain rapper at gunpoint days after sonâs birth
articles.summary: US Streamers News: Bluefaceâs livestream took a shocking turn on August 23 when armed police officers approached and detained the rapper during what was reportedly a swa.
articles.body: Blueface’s livestream took a shocking turn on August 23 when armed police officers approached and detained the rapper during what was reportedly a swatting call. Blueface, whose real name is Jonathan Porter, was seen following police orders, kneeling down and keeping his hands raised before officers put him in handcuffs. His girlfriend, Nevaeh Akira, was also at the scene with their newborn baby. The incident happened only five days after the couple welcomed their first child together, making the sudden police response even more alarming for viewers watching online.Blueface detained at gunpoint during livestream as police respondFootage shared online shows several police officers approaching Blueface during the incident. The rapper followed their instructions and got down on his knees with his hands raised.Officers then placed Blueface in handcuffs while they secured and searched the area. Akira was also seen holding the couple’s newborn son while officers searched her before moving her away from the main scene.There were no reports that Akira or the baby were hurt.The exact reason for the police response has not been confirmed by authorities. However, several claims about the incident quickly spread online.One claim said police were sent to King of Crabs, a seafood restaurant in Santa Clarita linked to Blueface, after someone reported a shooting. Another video appeared to include an emergency caller claiming that Blueface had punched his fiancée in the face.Neither claim had been officially confirmed at the time of reporting. Authorities had also not released a public statement explaining why officers arrived with weapons drawn.The incident ended with Blueface being detained while police checked the situation.Blueface and Nevaeh Akira had welcomed their newborn days earlierThe police incident happened just five days after Blueface and Akira became parents.The couple welcomed their son, Johnathan Jamall Porter Jr., on August 18. Akira’s labor was also livestreamed on Kick, making the birth a major moment for their online audience.Because of this, seeing the rapper and his family surrounded by police so soon afterward shocked many viewers.The latest incident is also not the first time Blueface has faced a suspected swatting call. In July, police responded to his home in Canyon Country after a report claimed that a woman had been shot at the property.Blueface was livestreaming on Kick when officers arrived. Deputies later found that nobody had been injured and determined that the report was a swatting call. The rapper was briefly detained before being released after police confirmed there was no shooting.Swatting happens when someone makes a false emergency report to send armed police to another person’s location. Online creators and celebrities can become targets because these incidents can happen while they are livestreaming.For now, the reason behind the latest police response remains unclear. Authorities have not confirmed the claims spreading online, leaving viewers waiting for more information about what happened during Blueface’s livestream.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Lindsay Clancy trial: Judge rejects mistrial plea after psychologist's Catholic faith remarks
articles.summary: US News: A judge has rejected a defence request for a mistrial in the case of Lindsay Clancy, who is accused of killing her three young children in Massachuset.
articles.body: A judge has rejected a defence request for a mistrial in the case of Lindsay Clancy, who is accused of killing her three young children in Massachusetts, after a prosecution psychologist brought her Catholic faith into his testimony.The ruling came as Clancy's closely watched triple-murder trial neared its conclusion, with closing arguments expected Wednesday, according to NBC News.Defence seeks mistrial over Catholic faith remarksForensic psychologist Kirk Heilbrun was testifying for the prosecution when he referred to Clancy's Roman Catholic upbringing while discussing her state of mind at the time of the killings.Heilbrun mentioned Clancy's statement that she told her children to âGo to Godâ before killing them and questioned her about Catholic teachings on suicide.The defence immediately objected, and attorney Kevin Reddington moved for a mistrial, accusing the prosecution of improperly introducing religion into the trial.Judge Sullivan rejected the mistrial request but ordered jurors to disregard Heilbrun's remarks about Clancy's faith and Catholic theology.âThe religion that the defendant was raised is absolutely an inappropriate area of testimony,â the judge was quoted as saying by CNN. He also instructed jurors not to consider the remarks.Psychologist questions psychosis claimHeilbrun's testimony otherwise focused on whether Clancy was experiencing psychosis when she killed her children, Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months, at their Duxbury home in January 2023.He said Clancy claimed she heard a male voice telling her to kill herself and her children, but noted that she did not report hearing the voice before or after the killings.The psychologist said the account was more consistent with an intrusive thought than a command hallucination and described the killings as âaltruistic filicideâ â killing children out of a belief that they would suffer without the parent, CNN reported.Defence says postpartum psychosis left her unawareClancy, 36, has pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity to three counts of murder. She has admitted killing her children, but her defence says she was in the grip of severe postpartum mental illness and could not appreciate the wrongfulness of her actions.Prosecutors argue that while Clancy had mental health problems, she understood what she was doing and deliberately killed her children before attempting suicide.Closing arguments are expected Wednesday as the trial moves towards a verdict.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Musk's data centers push out family that's owned land for generations
articles.summary: A plant in Southaven, Mississippi, that powers Elon Musk's SpaceXAI data centers in the area has sparked backlash from residents concerned about noise and ai...
articles.body:
On a 2-acre property in Mississippi , 52-year-old Krystal Polk's family lived off the land for generations, raising chickens and pigs, growing onions and herbs and trading their peaches for pears.

The land, on the border with Tennessee in the city of Southaven, was her family's survival, Polk said. "We lived a very simplistic life," she told CBS News.

While life there may have been simple in Polk's view, the circumstances surrounding her home rarely ever were. Her family acquired the property "before people of color were allowed to have land," she said, and it's been passed down for four generations. When Polk's parents first moved in, they discovered "KKK" scrawled at the bottom of the hill of their property, she said.

Holding on to the land was made more difficult a year ago when a noisy neighbor appeared across the street — a power plant so loud, it drove the family away. Since then, the land has sat mostly empty, occupied only by an unrelenting hum.

The plant, which is powering Elon Musk's SpaceXAI data centers in the Memphis area, has sparked backlash from Southaven residents concerned about noise and air pollution. A petition by the resident-run Safe and Sound Coalition calling to shut down the power plant has over 1,400 signatures.

Polk said she remembers when she could hear the birds chirping at her family home. Now, she said the plant's "constant roaring" lingers in her ears even after she leaves.

"It's like you're in the middle of the airport where the planes are taking off, but they never take off," she said.

SpaceXAI, formerly known as xAI, recently said in a July press release that it is investing millions of dollars in sound walls and silencers with "advanced quieting technologies" around the plant. Southaven residents have told CBS News that one sound wall installed so far has provided little reprieve from the noise.

Over the course of two years, Musk has expanded his footprint in the Memphis region starting with the construction of his Colossus 1 data center just north of Southaven in 2024. By January 2026, two more data centers were announced. This July, Musk quietly confirmed the construction of another local data center, "Minihard," in a reply to a post on his platform X.

Musk's SpaceXAI projects will total more than $20 billion in investments to Southaven, which Mississippi Gov. Tate Reeves said in a press release will "bring amazing opportunities to its residents for generations."

But for Polk, the development has meant a new kind of strain on her family.

"We don't know the future," she said. "So we're not sure what to invest into it."

Polk moved away from the family home after getting married, and for years, it bounced between relatives. It was where Polk churned her own ice cream as a child, held her rehearsal dinner when she got married and hosted the holidays each year.

"We gathered there and we thanked God for what we had," she said. "It was always a celebration."

She planned to return as a retiree and eventually pass the property down to her children. But now, those plans have been put on hold. Apart from the "24/7" noise, Polk said she and her family have asthma and are concerned about fumes from the gas turbines at the plant.

"I'm afraid that we will be the ones that everyone looks back on and says, 'Hey, remember they tried to tell us that these things were hazardous to our health and causing harm,'" Polk said. "I'm afraid that we're going to be those casualties."

The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People and other groups sued xAI and its subsidiary MZX Tech in April, alleging that the plant "emits significant amounts of harmful pollutants."

In June, SpaceXAI filed a motion to dismiss the case, and the Department of Justice also moved to intervene and dismiss the case. The Justice Department said in a statement that the matter "concerns national security and Mississippi's lawful action regarding permitting" and that the NAACP's lawsuit "could hinder the War Department's use of AI for national defense."

CBS News reached out to SpaceXAI multiple times for comment and has not heard back.

The company has entered into an agreement with the Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality that includes removing the 69 temporary turbines at the plant and replacing them with 41 permanent turbines over the course of a year.

But a study conducted by EmPower Analytics Group, an independent consulting firm that provides scientific analysis of the health impact of AI infrastructure, found that the plan to install dozens of gas turbines would increase air pollution in the area and would be concentrated in communities that are disproportionately Black.

The Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality said in a statement that it doesn't comment on "third-party reports or matters involved in pending litigation" and that it "remains committed to carrying out its responsibility to protect public health and the environment through implementation and enforcement of applicable state and federal environmental laws and regulations."

MDEQ said that as part of the permitting process, MZX Tech was required to demonstrate that the proposed facility would not violate air quality standards.

Still, residents are not convinced. Shannon Samsa, a 27-year-old physician assistant living in Southaven, is concerned about the plant's impact on her community's health. She's become an outspoken advocate against the plant, speaking up at city meetings and leading the Safe and Sound Coalition as its director.

"It's not just my neighbors, it's not just my family and friends, it's my future patients," she said. "It's also a huge healthcare issue."

As SpaceXAI extends its reach in the region, the future of Polk's property hangs in the balance. Some companies have expressed interest in purchasing it.

Polk said she was approached by real estate firm Cushman & Wakefield with an offer. After multiple "nos" over the course of weeks, she said she eventually filed a Better Business Bureau complaint, accusing the company of harassment and manipulation.

In the complaint, reviewed by CBS News, Polk alleged the firm's Tennessee branch tried to coerce her into agreeing to services.

Cushman & Wakefield, in response to the complaint, said it was exploring the potential acquisition of Polk's land on behalf of a client, who was not identified. The firm confirmed it made multiple attempts to contact Polk "by phone, text and written correspondence," but denied engaging in "harassment, pressure tactics, or inappropriate conduct." CBS News reached out to Cushman & Wakefield and did not receive a response.

Polk said the company has not reached out since she filed the complaint. She declined to disclose Cushman & Wakefield's offer, but said that "it was not worth anything."

Selling the land is complicated — keeping it was her father's dying wish, Polk said.

"He asked me to please keep it as much as I could within reason," she said. "I'm not sure if you could offer a value."

articles.title: Two unvaccinated people die of measles in Pennsylvania
articles.summary: Cases in the US have hit the highest point since the virus was eliminated, as vaccination rates decline.
articles.body:
Two people who were not vaccinated against measles have died of the virus in Pennsylvania, health officials said.

The state has seen 393 cases of the highly contagious virus this year, as infections across the US have hit the highest point in 35 years.

Eighty-five percent of kindergarten-age students in Lancaster County, where the recent deaths occurred, are vaccinated against measles - well below the 95% rate needed for herd immunity to limit the spread and protect immunocompromised people.

Last year, two unvaccinated children in Texas died from a measles outbreak that infected over 1,000 people, primarily children.

"This is a serious and a growing problem across our country and in our commonwealth," Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro said in a news conference on Tuesday. "This illness and death from measles is completely preventable."

He added that the mumps, measles and rubella (MMR) vaccine was the best tool to protect against illness and death.

Officials said they would not share any additional information on the identities of those who died, including if they were children, who have face a higher risk of death and complications from measles.

The US has seen 2,777 confirmed cases of measles in 2026, just seven months into the year, up from last year's high of 2,289.

The rising number of cases comes as vaccine hesitancy in the US has increased in recent years, leading to lower immunisation rates. The US recommends two shots to children between ages one and six, which is 97% effective in protecting against the illness.

Earlier this month, President Donald Trump signed an executive order that calls for fewer childhood vaccinations and recommends splitting the MMR vaccine into three separate shots. Public health experts worry the order will cause confusion about an already safe and effective vaccine and prove costly.

The executive order came after Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr took a number of steps to remake US vaccine policies over the past year, including the childhood vaccination schedule. Many of the changes were blocked by a federal judge earlier this year.

A vaccine skeptic, Kennedy has shared mixed messaging on the MMR vaccine, at times endorsing it and other times sharing unproven claims about its safety.

Speaking on Tuesday, Shapiro said he spoke with Kennedy over the phone that morning and that he had offered to send staff from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Shapiro said he was "very blunt" with Kennedy about vaccinations.

"I made very clear that his actions and the rhetoric that's coming from this administration are having a negative impact on communities across America ... that there's real life consequences to spreading misinformation," Shapiro said.

The US is on track to lose its status of having eliminated measles, which will be determined by a panel in November. Canada lost its status last year.

articles.title: 7 hours for lip gloss, 2 hours for a croissant: Welcome to line culture, where flexing how long you waited is part of the fun
articles.summary: Waiting in line is cool again. For young people chasing viral products and experiences, the inconvenience may be part of what makes it special.
articles.body:
At 5:30 in the morning, Kristen and her sister arrived in Newport, Rhode Island, armed with a blanket, snacks and a suspicion that Hailey Bieber might show up. The 22-year-old had driven an hour from Connecticut for the first day of the summer pop-up from Rhode, a special event from Bieber's massively popular beauty brand, celebrating a seasonal drop . The doors wouldn't open until 11 a.m. Kristen had never done anything like this before and she expected the hours to drag. But that didn't end up being the case.

"We were just making friends with the people around us," she tells Yahoo. "It was really cool to hear everyone's story on why they were there, where they're coming from."

Even after the doors finally opened — five and a half hours after they arrived — Kristen was still about 40th in line and had another hour and a half to wait. But the waiting had begun to turn into something else.

Security handed out wristbands. Newport coffee shop Nitro Bar passed out caramelized banana lattes , a nod to a drink Bieber had talked about making at home. There were bingo cards with the chance to win free products. "The little surprises that came along the way got people so excited," says Kristen. "And that's when I was like, OK, waiting was worth it."

Kristen ended up nabbing a pocket bronzer, two lip liners and lip glosses, and an exclusive Newport Rhode hoodie. She returned again the next day and spent another six hours outside the pop-up, hoping Bieber would appear. (She didn't. But cinnamon rolls were passed around for attendees.)

Today's young people came of age in an era of one-click everything, where almost anything can be ordered to your doorstep in a matter of 48 hours. Given that fact, spending the better part of one (or two) days waiting outside a store sounds almost absurd.

Yet this summer, lines have solidified themselves as a recurring feature in the lives of young people chasing after trendy consumer products: they've formed outside beauty pop-ups and bakeries, artist activations, coffee and matcha shops and stores carrying the latest cult item. Getting the thing that you want, line enthusiasts say, is almost more special because you had to prove that you really wanted it.

The merchandise might be available elsewhere. But acquiring the thing isn't necessarily the point. "People don't wait in line for products anymore," Ryan Glick, founder of Coffee N' Clothes (CNC) , a brand-experience agency that produces more than 200 events a year, tells Yahoo. "They're waiting in line to be a part of a moment."

Glick has seen the phenomenon evolve from both sides of the rope. He started his company by organizing meet-ups for online communities and eventually grew it into a business that helps brands across fashion, beauty, entertainment and tech produce IRL experiences. "In a world where digital made everything available to everyone instantly, showing up is proof that you're physically there for something that mattered," he says.

There may also be something psychological happening as those hours tick by too, according to Derek D. Rucker , a professor of marketing at Northwestern University, who points to the concept of "effort justification" — the tendency to value something more once we've invested time or work into getting it. "The more effort we have to put into something, the more we justify it as, 'It must be worth it,'" Rucker tells Yahoo.

Kristen could've waited for the Rhode products she wanted to arrive at Sephora. But the pop-up offered something Sephora couldn't. "It's just a cooler experience when you go to an event for it," she said. With only two U.S. pop-up locations at the time, being able to attend one made her "feel special."

That distinction — between buying something and being there — runs through the line phenomenon.

When Valeria Rose, 23, recently returned to Los Angeles after attending college in Santa Barbara, she went to Ariana Grande's Eternal Sunshine experience in West Hollywood. She had seen TikToks of fans arriving at 6 a.m. and not getting inside until mid-afternoon, so she strategically went on a weekday. She still waited nearly three hours.

The fan event was cool — there was a photo booth and a flower-covered wall where fans could leave Grande notes. But more importantly, Valeria went with a friend who wanted to be there as much as she did. "Having someone to chat with honestly makes the time go faster," she tells Yahoo.

Growing up near the entertainment industry, Valeria is a veteran of line culture. She's met people waiting in line for concerts, meet-and-greets and pop-ups — some of those friendships lasted long after the line disappeared. Returning to that ritual after years away from L.A. also offered an unexpected connection to her younger self.

"It was pretty funny that on my first day back home, I was waiting in line," she says. "I felt so connected to my past self."

On vacation in Arizona, Elizabeth and her sister had an open day and kept seeing Sablé Boulangerie, a viral bakery in Gilbert, on their TikTok feeds. They decided to see what the hype was about and spent an hour and 37 minutes in line to get their hands on a selection of pastries and the bakery's internet-famous chocolate chip cookie.

Around them, people worked on laptops, played games and sat in chairs. Families and groups of friends waited together. Chef Will Porter, whose social media presence has helped make the bakery a destination, briefly "walked the line" with a cameraman and bodyguards.

Elizabeth started filming mostly because she was curious how long the wait would take. The resulting video got 50,000 views, when most of her posts typically draw around 500.

"If you post about standing in a line and say how long you stood in the line, people can't wait to tell you how dumb you are in the comments," says Elizabeth. "It drives engagement. It's essentially easy rage bait."

It creates a strategically efficient cycle: A viral place attracts a crowd. The crowd creates a line. People film the line because it is remarkable. The resulting content reaches more people, who then want to see what could possibly be worth waiting for.

It's a marketing jackpot. Whether you encounter it in person or watch it unfold on TikTok, you're seeing dozens of people weigh whether something is really that valuable in real time. Timothy D. Malefyt , a marketing professor at Fordham University, calls that "embodied social proof" and it naturally gives observers FOMO, the feeling that the people in line "apparently know something I don't."

There is, Elizabeth admits, "a bit of excitement to try something that's trending and see for yourself if it's actually good." Going also gives you something to talk about when other people inevitably ask, "Was it worth it?"

In her case, yes — with a caveat. She still thinks about Sablé's pain suisse. "The pastries truly were delicious," she says, "but I wouldn't stand in that line again."

Of course, people stood in lines long before TikTok. There were Black Friday doorbusters, concert ticket sales and Supreme drops. Glick remembers waiting outside Supreme — which was created as more of a community space than a traditional retail store — with his mom as a kid.

What has changed may be how many ordinary products can now be transformed into events — and how quickly social media can create a craze around them.

In Iowa, Anna T., 40, found herself waking up before dawn to hunt for NeeDoh squishy toys with her 11-year-old daughter. A local children's boutique would announce "drop" dates for harder-to-find designs, prompting customers to line up before opening.

The first time Anna went, she waited in the snow for roughly two hours. On another trip, she and her daughter arrived at 6:15 a.m. for a 9 a.m. opening. Eventually, Anna took her daughter and two friends at 5 a.m. By then, the wait had become an event of its own. "The store owner came out around 7:30 a.m. and had music," she tells Yahoo. "The kids were dancing, and it was a very fun and lively experience."

For Anna's daughter, the inconvenience was novel — and part of the appeal. "She told me she really wanted to because she has never waited in line to buy anything before and she said she wanted to experience that," says Anna. That struck her. "We've waited in lines for a ride, but never for a material thing."

In a childhood shaped by online shopping and instant gratification, even the hassle is part of the charm. "When something is easily accessible, we tend to think anyone could get it and that it's not as special as things that took work, energy, time or were scarce," Elizabeth Schwab , a professor in the Business Psychology Division at The Chicago School, tells Yahoo.

But the hours spent waiting can offer something else that clicking "buy now" can't: doing it with others. "We enjoy feeling like we belong; that we've found our people and our community," Schwab says.

That would explain why, for Anna, the NeeDohs themselves were almost beside the point. "I don't do it for the actual item," she says. "For my daughter, it was about getting the trendy new item, but I know these are memories that she will be able to talk about with her kids one day. And all of it is a reason for us to spend time together."

There is a limit to the romance of waiting. Elizabeth, who waited nearly two hours outside the bakery, says her ceiling is an hour or two. Valeria questions the appeal of standing around for something as fleeting as a celebrity-branded smoothie. Glick cautions that brands shouldn't manufacture lines simply to appeal popular — a badly managed wait can just as easily backfire, he says.

And even the people willing to queue for hours know how irrational it can look from the outside. Perhaps that's what makes the line work.

Convenience has stripped away much of the friction that once surrounded buying something. The line puts some of it back, but with friends, anticipation, exclusivity and a story attached.

The most telling thing about this summer of lines may be that Anna's daughter didn't simply want the NeeDoh. She really wanted to wait for it.

articles.title: How Often Should You Replace Running Shoes? Podiatrists Explain
articles.summary: Running in worn-out shoes can lead to aches, pains and injuries. Podiatrists break down how many miles your running shoes should last and when it’s time for a new pair.
articles.body: We don’t always have the answers, but we have some people on speed dial who do — which is why we present to you our series FYI where we have experts explain if hair removal cream is actually bad, how often you should change your towels and more. Running shoes don’t last forever, even if they still look fine from the outside. Over time, the cushioning and support inside break down and running in shoes that have lost their structure can leave your feet, knees and joints unsupported, making you more prone to aches, pains and even injuries. The tricky part is that this breakdown happens gradually, so it’s easy to keep running in shoes that have quietly stopped doing their job. To find out exactly when it’s time to retire your running shoes — and what to watch for before your body starts sending its own warning signals — I talked to doctors who explained how mileage and body type factor into the equation. I’ve also rounded up some podiatrist- and editor-approved running shoes worth adding to your cart if you find that it’s time for a fresh pair. How often do running shoes need to be replaced? Most doctors say mileage is the clearest benchmark for retiring your running shoes. “In general, a running shoe should last somewhere between 300 and 500 miles,” says Dr. Dietmar Walter, head of podiatry at Stride Soles, a custom orthotics company. “However, the exact length depends on your weight, running surface and of course the shoe type.” Treadmills tend to be gentler on shoes, while consistently running on pavement or concrete can wear down cushioning a bit faster, since there’s less natural give to absorb the impact. Body weight in particular can make a dramatic difference in how quickly a shoe wears out. “I see many patients over 200 pounds only last 200 miles in their shoes, while someone under 140 pounds might last over 550 miles,” says Walter. That’s a gap of more than 350 miles between the two groups, underscoring why there’s no single mileage number that works for every runner — and why paying attention to how your shoes feel matters just as much as counting miles. What are signs you need to replace your running shoes? Mileage is a helpful guideline, but your body often sends signals before you hit a specific number. “A good sign that your shoes need replacing is if you are starting to get unexpected aches and pains — like achilles tendonitis, shin splints or plantar fascia pain,” says Dr. Milica McDowell, a doctor of physical therapy and co-author of Walk: Rediscover the Most Natural Way to Boost Your Health and Longevity ― One Step at a Time. If new discomfort starts creeping in during or after your runs, it’s worth taking a closer look at your shoes before the problem gets worse. Walter also says you can examine your shoe to look for signs of excessive wear. These are the things he says point to your shoes needing to be replaced: Look at the midsole: If it looks compressed, has striations (grooves or ridges) in it or has uneven wear, it’s likely time to replace the shoes.Check the inside back of your shoes: Look at where your achilles rests against the back of your shoes. If that area is torn or there is missing material, this is a major sign to replace your shoe as your foot is no longer being held securely as you run.Examine the bottom of your shoes: Simply checking the rubber at the bottom of your shoes is an easy way to see if there is excessive wear. If you notice foam through the bottom or areas where there is no tread, it’s likely time to replace your shoes. I also have flat feet and find that these have the perfect amount of arch support for me. articles.title: 9/11 victim's identity emerges nearly 25 years later after DNA breakthrough cracks mystery
articles.summary: A first-of-its-kind forensic genealogy technique helped New York City investigators identify a World Trade Center victim nearly 25 years after 9/11.
articles.body: Nearly 25 years after the Sept. 11 attacks, a family has finally received an answer after New York City investigators used a first-of-its-kind DNA and genealogy technique to identify a woman killed at the World Trade Center. The adult woman, whose name is being withheld at her family’s request, is the first World Trade Center victim identified through forensic investigative genetic genealogy, New York City officials announced Sunday. Her identification marks the 1,654th person identified from remains recovered after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, which killed 2,753 people in New York City. 9/11 MUSEUM CEO REFLECTS ON LASTING IMPACT OF TERROR ATTACKS AS AMERICA MARKS 250TH BIRTHDAY The breakthrough came through a collaboration between the Office of Chief Medical Examiner, and the NYPD’s Investigative Genetic Genealogy Squad. The technique pairs specialized DNA analysis with genealogy research to generate leads that are then confirmed through forensic testing. "As we approach the 25th anniversary of the horrific September 11 attacks, we honor the nearly 3,000 people whose lives were stolen that day," NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a statement. "We remain committed to the families who have spent 25 years waiting for answers." REMAINS FOUND IN UTAH DESERT 28 YEARS AGO WITH HELP OF A PSYCHIC FINALLY IDENTIFIED THROUGH DNA GENEALOGY Forensic investigative genetic genealogy has emerged as a powerful tool in cold cases, allowing investigators to trace family connections from DNA evidence and identify people who may otherwise have remained unknown. Chief Medical Examiner Dr. Graham said the new method could help advance the city’s long-running effort to identify those killed in the attacks. WOMAN FOUND IN SHALLOW GRAVE ID’D AFTER 44 YEARS AS MILLIONAIRE TIED TO ESTATE MURDER PLOT "This sacred commitment is propelled by our dedication to apply the most innovative scientific techniques," Graham said. "FIGG represents a promising new addition to our toolkit." Officials said they are also using renewed family outreach and continued DNA retesting to link recovered remains to victims already identified. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP But the work remains unfinished. About 1,099 World Trade Center victims, roughly 40% of those killed, have yet to be identified. The woman is the first newly identified World Trade Center victim since August 2025, officials said.

articles.title: Who does Iran trade with and what could Trump's 'economic D-Day' mean?
articles.summary: Iran is no stranger to US sanctions and has developed deep economic ties with several countries.
articles.body:
The US has said "the single greatest financial offensive ever" will help it and Israel end their ongoing war with Iran.

However, Iran is no stranger to these tactics.

The regime has faced near continuous US sanctions since the Islamic Revolution of 1979. In that time, it has developed deep trade ties with several countries which either have a history of ignoring US economic pressure themselves or cannot afford to stop trading with Iran.

As a result, Iran says it is "fully prepared" for the new US sanctions and many economists argue the impact of Washington's latest move will be limited.

So, who does Iran trade with? And could what the US has called an "economic D-Day" have any real impact on Iran?

China is the biggest buyer of Iranian goods, making up 26.9% of its exports in 2025, according data from the International Trade Centre (ITC), a subsidiary of the United Nations and the World Trade Organisation.

There a few caveats to ITC's data, which covers a period before the US-Israel war with Iran began.

First, several economists believe that even before the conflict started, a lot of Iranian oil sales, particularly to China, were underreported for political reasons.

Second, the ITC tallies Iran's exports using mostly the import numbers reported by its trading partners - owing to the difficulty in getting up to date export data from Iran.

Third, import data for some of Iran's trading partners, such as Iraq, is incomplete.

Despite this, Iranian trade's importance to China is clear from its response to the US announcement of "economic D-Day".

It said that it was firmly opposed to what it called "illegal unilateral sanctions", that economic pressure tactics would not help resolve problems and that Beijing would safeguard its own interests.

Turkey is another large trading partner of Iran, according to ITC data, but it has a much friendlier relationship with the US than China.

This puts it in a challenging position. The US has threatened to punish those who continue to trade with Iran as part of its economic pressure tactics.

However, economists point out that Turkey cannot stop trading with it without significant damage to its economy, which is already struggling with inflation running at 31.8%, according to official data .

In short, as the only Nato member to share a border with Iran, Turkey has to balance its relationship with military allies and maintaining a relationship with its close economic neighbour.

Like Turkey, Pakistan borders Iran and is one of its biggest export partners, according to ITC data, while also being keen to maintain a good relationship with the US.

But unlike Turkey, Pakistan's top export partner is instead the US, meaning it has more to lose from any economic punishment imposed by Washington.

It is also a key mediator in peace talks between the US and Iran, meaning a breakdown in its relationship with either country could make finding a solution to the conflict even more challenging.

The other complicating factor is that not all of Pakistan's trade with Iran is within the Pakistan government's control.

The BBC has seen evidence that oil is being smuggled across the border from Iran to Pakistan en masse by bikers , some as young as 15.

This was the case before the Iran war began, but data suggests the practice has picked up since.

And though the US and Pakistan's oil firms have pressured Pakistan's government to clamp down on the practice, it has struggled to police remote parts of the 900km border.

The BBC has previously asked the Iranian government to comment on the allegation that it is involved in the fuel smuggling. It did not respond.

Armenia is another major trading partner of Iran, according to the ITC data.

Where it differs the most from others is that its top export partner is Russia, which accounts for 34.9% of all goods sold by Armenia in 2025.

This is despite the fact that Russia has faced sanctions from the US and its allies since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

This suggests Armenia may be willing to continue trading with Iran despite mounting US pressure.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the sanctions against Iran will "tighten the noose and block every potential source of revenue".

Yet, many experts disagree. Advisory firm Oxford Economics said the direct impact on Iran's revenues would be "somewhat of a damp squib".

Ali Vaez, deputy director at the International Crisis Group, said: "Anything that moves in Iran has already been sanctioned by multiple layers of sanctions, in fact.

"So the question now is one of enforcement. Does the United States have what it takes to impose fines and levies on countries that continue to trade with Iran?"

He noted how the US started an economic war with China, Iran's biggest trading partner, last year but "backed out of it".

Former senior advisor at the state department Aya Ibrahim said the US's overreliance on them "incentivises countries to find ways around that system".

She also raised concerns that the sanctions may have the biggest affect on people, rather than economies, as they "deny people necessities to stay alive".

Meanwhile, global markets have had a muted response to the announcement.

Global oil prices fell following the announcement, but are still far higher than pre-war levels.

Stock traders were even less moved by the news, with the major indexes of the biggest companies listed in the US, Europe, and Asia barely shifting.

The US will has a way to go before it convinces economists, investors, and the nations trading with Iran that its sanctions threat is to be taken seriously.

articles.title: Swedish military seeks to take over Russian-owned estate near naval base
articles.summary: The armed forces request the seizure of the plot near Muskö Naval Base citing threats from Russian drones.
articles.body:
Sweden's armed forces have asked the government to expropriate a Russia-owned property near a naval base on security grounds.

The military requested the seizure of the beach plot near Muskö base in Stockholm archipelago, citing "the threat from Russian drones and the ownership situation of the property".

Swedish reports say a businessman with links to the Russian state, has been building a luxury house on Muskö island – although his wife, who holds both Russian and Swedish citizenship, is the registered owner.

Two years ago, Sweden ended two centuries of military non-alignment and joined Nato because of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

In its statement, the military said the location had "unique conditions for strengthening the defence of Muskö Naval Base, particularly against drones".

The development of Russian drone warfare has "changed the threat landscape for Sweden", the military added.

Public broadcaster SVT said the property has been "a thorn in the armed forces' side".

Defence Minister Pål Jonson said the country needed to "make sure there's no risk of anyone gaining visibility into the site or any kind of tactical edge", Sweden's TV4 reported.

The armed forces' statement quoted Chief of the Defence Staff Carl-Johan Edström as saying that Sweden was "facing the most serious security situation since the end of World War Two".

It is unclear whether the Russian businessman is currently living in Sweden.

His wife is reported to have owned the property since 2017.

articles.title: Did India hit Kirana Hills during Op Sindoor? Ex-CDS Anil Chauhan clears air
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Former Chief of Defence Staff Anil Chauhan on Tuesday said India may have hit Pakistan's Kirana Hills during Operation Sindoor last year, b.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Former Chief of Defence Staff Anil Chauhan on Tuesday said India may have hit Pakistan's Kirana Hills during Operation Sindoor last year, but the strike was unintentional.Speaking at the âVIMARSHâ event on Operation Sindoor and its aftermath at the Vivekanand International Foundation, Chauhan said Indian loitering missions sent to search for radars around Sargodha ran out of fuel and ended up hitting Kirana Hills -- a site associated with Pakistan's nuclear facilities."At occasions, it's been asked whether Kirana Hills were hit or not, which is where their (Pakistan's) nuclear facilities are... Before those strikes, we had sent in a lot of loitering missions at Sargodha and Kirana Hills is about 10 kilometers north of Sargodha," Chauhan said."So the loitering mission is looking for radars which are in and around Sargodha, and it has a lifetime, which means it will loiter for about 2 hours and once it does not find a target, it comes down and hits somewhere. It must have come and hit one of those hills. So that could be one of the reasons as to what people asked, because Pakistani media also showed some kind of images in which there was smoke coming out from Kirana Hills," he added.Chauhan also revealed details of another episode during the operation, saying the Air Chief sought his approval to strike Sargodha after Pakistan requested talks. However the target was changed to Bholari due to bad weather."Once the Pakistanis had picked up the phone and said they wanted to talk at about 10 AM. The Air Chief asked me whether he should strike Sargodha, I said, Go ahead. I said, could you please identify two more targets, so one of the targets he identified was Skardu," Chauhan said."We gave a yes, but after some time, the weather was bad over it and they had to change over to Bholari," he added.During his address, Chauhan also stressed that military decisions involve varying levels of risk and must be assessed against the political objectives they are intended to achieve."Each option has a certain kind of risk involved in it, and also it will satisfy the political need for which it was to be used. So, itâs an interplay between risk and attainment of political objectives," he said.Chauhan said the operation remains relevant nearly 15 months after its major active phase ended. He said its assessment should take into account deficiencies identified during the operation, measures taken to address them and the changing nature of warfare.He added that these factors, along with wider global uncertainties, are creating new challenges for military planners.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Target apologises for 'offensive' children Halloween costume after backlash
articles.summary: The retailer says the costume is "hurtful for Black guests, team members and partners", without providing further details.
articles.body:
American retail giant Target has withdrawn a Halloween costume from sale after critics on social media said it resembled a racist caricature.

Describing the costume as "offensive", the store said in a statement that it was "hurtful for our Black guests, team members and partners", without providing further details.

Images circulating online show a costume sold as the "Kids' Glows Under Blacklight Circus Clown Halloween Costume", and customers and others on social media say it evokes blackface and minstrel shows.

"As a company, we know we got this wrong, and we are deeply sorry," Target said. "The costume is offensive and should never have been part of our assortment."

"Removing the costume is an important first step, and the company is looking closely at how this happened and what needs to change to ensure this won't happen again," Target said.

The BBC asked Target about the costume in question, but the retailer declined to comment further.

Target has recently faced supply shortages and backlash over its decision to end its diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) targets.

The company was also criticised over its handling of products in its Pride Collection in 2023.

The store is known for its affordable clothing and a wide range of groceries, household goods, electronics and toys.

articles.title: Air Force officer who died in Alaska plane crash remembered as 'positive leader'
articles.summary: The Air Force identified 2nd Lt. Leah Borsich, 23, as a victim of the deadly Alaska charter plane crash that killed all eight on board near Cape Newenham.
articles.body: A 23-year-old Air Force officer killed alongside seven others in a charter plane crash in remote western Alaska last week is being remembered as a "positive leader" who served with "professionalism, compassion and purpose." The Air Force identified 2nd Lt. Leah R. Borsich on Monday as one of the victims of the Aug. 20 crash near the Cape Newenham Long Range Radar Site Airport, about 450 miles west-southwest of Anchorage. Borsich was a project programmer with the 611th Civil Engineer Squadron at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson. "Lt. Borsich was a positive leader who brought tremendous energy and enthusiasm to our command," Col. Timothey Meerstein, commander of the Pacific Air Forces Regional Support Center, said in a statement. TWO US ARMY CORPS OF ENGINEERS EMPLOYEES AMONG 8 KILLED IN ALASKA CHARTER PLANE CRASH "She led with professionalism, compassion and purpose, and her presence strengthened the bonds between the people around her," Meerstein said. "She made a lasting impact on our team, and we are grateful for her service and commitment to our nation." The Cessna 441 was carrying two pilots and six passengers when it crashed west of Cape Newenham at about 12:15 p.m. Thursday. All eight people aboard were killed. The charter plane had taken off from Ted Stevens Anchorage International Airport and was headed to Cape Newenham when it crashed during its second approach to the gravel runway in heavy fog, according to federal officials. The pilots could not see the runway and were flying by instruments, Clint Johnson, the National Transportation Safety Board’s Alaska region chief, said Friday. They aborted their first landing attempt because of poor visibility before crashing on the second approach. An observation system near the airport reported fog and visibility of about 10 miles shortly before the crash. About 15 minutes later, visibility had fallen to less than a quarter-mile, according to the National Weather Service. Search teams later found fragmented wreckage from the twin-engine plane, also known as a Cessna Conquest. The Air Force said an Army member, contractors and crew members with Anchorage-based airplane charter company Security Aviation were also among those killed. "We also mourn the loss of our Army and contractor teammates and extend our deepest appreciation to the Security Aviation aircrew, whose professionalism and dedication are vital to our mission," Meerstein said. "Their service and sacrifice will not be forgotten." Security Aviation, which operated the flight, said it was "heartbroken" by the crash. "Our hearts go out to the families, friends and loved ones of those who were lost," the company said in a statement posted to Facebook. "We extend our deepest condolences to them and to everyone affected by this devastating tragedy." Security Aviation thanked the military, Alaska Rescue Coordination Center and search-and-recovery teams that responded after the crash. The company said it is cooperating with the investigation and would not speculate about the cause. "Our focus at this time is on those who are grieving and on supporting our employees and others affected by this tremendous loss," the company said. In addition to the pilots, those aboard included two U.S. Army Corps of Engineers employees and four contractors. Two of the contractors worked for Calista Brice, which provides construction, engineering, logistics and other services in remote areas. ARMY IDENTIFIES 2 PILOTS KILLED IN APACHE HELICOPTER CRASH NEAR FORT HOOD DURING TRAINING EXERCISE The Army Corps said its employees were part of a "project delivery team en route to a project site in support of the U.S. Air Force." Officials have not said what work the group was traveling to perform. Cape Newenham is part of a network of remote radar sites that monitors aircraft operating in Alaska’s airspace and along its borders. The site, built in the 1950s as part of an early-warning network against a potential Soviet attack, now monitors the skies off Alaska’s coast in the direction of Russia, North Korea and China. Borsich’s name was released after her family had been notified. The Alaska State Troopers will release the names of the victims who were not affiliated with the Department of War, the Air Force said. Lt. Gen. Robert Davis, who leads Alaskan Command, the Alaskan North American Aerospace Defense Command Region and Eleventh Air Force, previously described those aboard as "dedicated professionals carrying out a vital mission in a demanding environment." "This is a devastating loss for our military family and the communities we serve," Davis said after the crash. articles.title: CIA chief travels to Moscow for unannounced talks, US media reports
articles.summary: Flight tracking data confirms an American military aircraft travelled to Russia from the US via Latvia on Tuesday.
articles.body:
The head of the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) has travelled to Moscow for unannounced talks, the BBC's US news partner CBS has reported.

John Ratcliffe reportedly arrived in the Russian capital earlier on Tuesday. Neither Washington or Moscow have confirmed the nature of the visit or who he was due to meet.

In-person talks between high-level American and Russian officials are rare.

Flight tracking data confirmed a large US military aircraft travelled to Russia from the US via Latvia on Tuesday. It departed later on Tuesday.

BBC News has contacted the CIA, the White House and Pentagon for comment.

Footage posted on social media showed the C-17 transport plane approaching Moscow's Vnukovo international airport.

It departed Riga airport at 05:50 GMT and appeared to have landed in the Russian capital at around 07:04 GMT, according to data from FlightRadar24. It returned to Riga shortly before 17:00 GMT.

Footage on social media also purported to show a diplomatic motorcade travelling through Moscow.

Ahead of the trip, the US told Ukraine that a senior delegation would be travelling to Moscow and asked Kyiv to suspend strikes until they had left, a senior Ukrainian official told CBS.

The trip is thought to be Ratcliffe's first trip to Russia as CIA director, although he has maintained contact with his intelligence counterparts in Moscow.

John Foreman, who served as a British military attaché to Moscow between 2019 and 2022, told Radio 4's PM programme that the visit could be focused on "escalation management" given speculation recent drone activity in Germany could be linked to Russia .

He said: "The Americans don't normally send such a high ranking official to Moscow unannounced at short notice unless something is up."

Foreman said the trip could also concern the release of US detainees currently being held in Russia.

Ratcliffe played a role in negotiations for the release of Russian-American citizen Ksenia Karelina, who was jailed in Russia for over a year after being accused of providing support to Ukraine.

The CIA was also involved in a 2024 prisoner swap deal with Russia that saw the release of Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich, as well as former US marine Paul Whelan and Russian-American journalist Alsu Kurmasheva.

The US has had strained relations with Russia since it launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Since then, Russia has been isolated on the world stage and faced international economic sanctions.

Ratcliffe appears to be one of the highest-ranking US officials to visit the country during President Donald Trump's second term.

Trump met Russian President Vladimir Putin at a summit in Alaska last year but the meeting did not lead to a breakthrough. Subsequent US-led peace talks between Russia and Ukraine appear to have stalled.

Additional reporting by Washington correspondent Daniel Bush and BBC Verify

articles.title: Archaeologists found a 7,000-year-old pit packed with beaver bones; it reveals how Europe's first farmers used animal fur
articles.summary: Europe News: Archaeologists in Germany have uncovered a Stone Age pit near Alsleben, Saxony-Anhalt, containing the bones of at least twelve beavers, offering an un.
articles.body: Archaeologists in Germany have uncovered a Stone Age pit near Alsleben, Saxony-Anhalt, containing the bones of at least twelve beavers, offering an unusually vivid window into how Europe's earliest farmers exploited animal fur. The roughly 7,000-year-old feature was first unearthed in 2024 during surveys ahead of construction of the SuedOstLink power line, and has now been dated to between 4935 and 4787 BC, placing it within the Linear Pottery culture.The bones, described by researchers as "exceptionally well preserved and mostly unfragmented," show no anatomical connection to one another, suggesting the beavers were skinned and their carcasses left to decompose before the remains were finally gathered and buried together. Excavated by the State Office for Heritage Management and Archaeology (LDA) of Saxony-Anhalt, the find points to a deliberate, organised hunting episode, and hints at the surprisingly elaborate fur clothing worn by some of the continent's first farming communities.7,000-year-old beaver bones found along a major power line routeThe find emerged during preparatory archaeological surveys for the SuedOstLink, a major high-voltage direct current power line being built across Saxony-Anhalt. Investigations in the Salzland district were carried out by the State Office for Heritage Management and Archaeology (LDA) of Saxony-Anhalt, working closely with grid operator 50Hertz ahead of construction work along the route.The power line stretches roughly 170 kilometres through the state, running largely alongside the A14 and A9 motorways and cutting through what the LDA describes as old settlement land with exceptionally fertile soils. This has meant an unusually high concentration of archaeological sites requiring excavation and documentation before building work can proceed, and it was this process that first brought the pit to light near Alsleben in 2024.How archaeologists found a beaver bone pit near the Saale RiverThe site itself sits above the Saale River, at the point where the power line is due to cross beneath it using a trenchless tunnelling method. According to the press release by the State Office for Heritage Management and Archaeology Saxony-Anhalt, the area "had already been chosen as a settlement site in the Neolithic period (New Stone Age) and was also used during the Bronze and Iron Ages," making it a long-favoured spot for human occupation across millennia.Amid a dense scatter of postholes, storage pits and burial sites, one feature caught researchers' attention. Archaeologists describe an "initially inconspicuous-looking pit, approximately 80 centimetres in diameter," which turned out to be tightly packed with animal bone. The distinctive orange-to-reddish-brown teeth scattered through the fill immediately identified the remains as beaver. A flint tool found near the surface of the deposit hinted at an early date, prompting the team to lift the entire feature as a soil block for careful excavation under laboratory conditions.Why the 7,000-year-old beaver pit belonged to the Linear Pottery cultureRadiocarbon analysis has since pinned the pit firmly to between 4935 and 4787 BC, placing it within the Linear Pottery culture, one of the earliest farming societies to spread across central Europe. Crucially, the bone assemblage is unusually pure: it consists exclusively of beaver remains, and the bones themselves are described as "exceptionally well preserved and mostly unfragmented."Skull evidence points to a minimum of twelve individual beavers, spanning a wide range of ages from under a year old to more than eight years. Yet the bones show no anatomical connection to one another, and several elements are missing altogether, strong evidence, researchers say, that the carcasses were already fully skeletonised by the time they were finally buried in the pit.How the beaver bones reveal a deliberate hunting and fur-making processTaken together, the evidence points to a single, deliberate hunting episode rather than gradual accumulation over time. The LDA suggests the beavers were hunted along the Saale, skinned for their pelts, and their carcasses then left to decompose elsewhere before the disarticulated bones were finally gathered and disposed of in the pit, a two-stage process that speaks to a surprisingly organised approach to fur production.For researchers, the implications go well beyond hunting technique. As the LDA notes, the find "not only points to specialised hunting strategies in the early Neolithic period, but also allows us to draw conclusions about the clothing worn during this time, which we can imagine to have been quite elaborate." It is a rare direct link between a single archaeological deposit and the everyday material culture, in this case, warm, durable fur garments, of some of Europe's earliest farming communities.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
