articles.title: A New Jersey artist bought a 600-square-foot cabin in 1989 and kept adding to it; 37 years later, Luna Parc is a 5,000-square-foot home, studio and living artwork still being built
articles.summary: US News: When Ricky Boscarino came across a small 600-square-foot cabin in the woods in New Jersey in 1988, he saw more than just a place to live. A year later.
articles.body: When Ricky Boscarino came across a small 600-square-foot cabin in the woods in New Jersey in 1988, he saw more than just a place to live. A year later, he began transforming it into what would become his largest work in progress called Luna Parc.More than three decades later, the property in Sandyston Township has grown into a 5,000-square-foot home, studio and working art environment. According to SPACES Archives, the property now has 11 levels and 15 rooms, with each part reflecting Boscarino's work as an artist and craftsman.Boscarino, also known as Ricky of Luna Parc, comes from an artistic family. His family history, according to the Luna Parc website, goes back to the time of the Medici. He has continued that connection through his own work in metal, clay, glass, wood and cement.He graduated from the Rhode Island School of Design in 1982. His interest in creating unusual and detailed objects had developed much earlier. As a young student, he was recognised for making carefully crafted dioramas, including scenes of cockroaches in beauty salons and nativity scenes.Cabin became life-sized artworkBoscarino started transforming the New Jersey cabin in 1989. What began as a 600-square-foot structure eventually became a much larger space that combines his home and atelier.SPACES Archives describes Luna Parc as a personal home, working studio, living classroom and community artist space. The property has continued to develop as Boscarino has added new elements and used different materials and objects throughout the site.The entrance itself reflects this approach. A ferrocement structure welcomes visitors to the property and has been named the 'Artichoke Portico' by Boscarino.Inside, the rooms have their own themes and collections. The kitchen, for example, is decorated with milk tabs and nearly 20,000 wine corks placed along the walls. Other spaces include the Hall of Hats, Nature Lab, a weaving studio, a mosaiced bathroom and the Asia Room.The Asia Room contains a set of doors that are almost 200 years old. These objects are part of the wider collection that Boscarino has built into the property over the years.Objects from around the worldBoscarino is both an artist and a collector. He has travelled to more than 40 countries and brought back a practice or item from each place, incorporating them into Luna Parc.One of the spaces inside the home is the Ballroom. It contains Morse code messages, a real human skeleton and painted portraits created by Boscarino.The Ballroom is used to host artists and students for lectures and readings about different ways of working as an artist.As the house rises upwards, the spaces continue to change. Boscarino's bedroom is on the seventh level. At the top is the Sky Walk, decorated with whirlygigs and kinetic sculptures.From the Sky Walk, there is a view across the property and the garden. The outdoor area includes a cobalt blue bottle house and a garden designed to light up at night.There is also a small purple chapel on the property. It is surrounded by a fence made from crutches that Boscarino created in honour of his grandfather.The Chapel of the Saints and the crutch fence commemorate an event that Boscarino's grandfather witnessed as a child. According to the SPACES account, his grandfather saw a young man regain the ability to walk in front of him.Young artists learn at Luna ParcThe property is not only Boscarino's home and studio. Beyond the garden and chapel is his Atelier, where he works with interns who are young local artists.The programme gives them an opportunity to learn his techniques and craft. It also aims to show them another way of living and working as an artist.This part of Luna Parc became more formally organised in 2015, when Boscarino established the Luna Parc Atelier Foundation Inc. The foundation is an official non-profit.The foundation's programme also focuses on helping apprentices develop practical skills. According to the Luna Parc website, it âteaches apprentices hand working and business skills necessary to succeed as self-supporting artists,â while also caring for the home and its future.Luna Parc is not generally open to the public for tours. SPACES notes that visits are limited to certain Open House days.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Trump says all mines cleared from Strait of Hormuz
articles.summary: Iran has closed the vital waterway since the beginning of the conflict causing wild fluctuations in oil prices worldwide.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has said that the US Navy has removed or detonated all mines in the Strait of Hormuz - the vital waterway which Iran has largely closed since the beginning of the war in the Middle East.

"Iran has been notified that any ship or boat placing new mines will be immediately and systematically destroyed," Trump said in a post on his Truth Social platform.

Closure of the strait has caused wild fluctuations in the price of oil on world markets. Trump has often said the US has control of the area - but Iran has fired against vessels it says have sought to cross without its permission.

Some 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to transit the Strait of Hormuz before the war, which began on 28 February with US and Israeli air strikes against Iran.

In addition to closing the strait, Iran retaliated against Israel and against US bases in the region as well as US Arab allies in the Gulf.

A ceasefire aimed at facilitating talks to end the war has collapsed and there has been intermittent exchange of fire between the US and Iran.

However, this week the US announced a raft of economic sanctions against Iran.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that any nation financially partnering with Iran would be isolated.

Iran and the US signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) in June - a 14-point document which set a 60-day deadline to reach a deal on the Strait of Hormuz, before substantial negotiations on resolving the nuclear issue - allegations that Iran is building a nuclear weapon, which Tehran has consistently denied.

However, that deadline has now expired and talks have collapsed leading to the new US sanctions that Trump believes will lead to the collapse of the Iranian regime.

Iran has been under sanctions for most of the time since the founding of the Islamic Republic in 1979 and Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh said Tehran was "fully prepared" for the wider sanctions, which he added would lead to "another defeat" for the US.

Its economy, however, has suffered as a result of the war - and a blockade of Iranian ports that the US has been maintaining for weeks not to allow trade to continue.

On Tuesday, China - the biggest buyer of Iranian oil - said it was firmly opposed to what it called the US's "illegal unilateral sanctions" and would take "all necessary measures" to safeguard its rights.

The US announcement comes ahead of planned talks between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping next month.

Washington is likely to be wary of potential retaliation from Beijing, which processes the majority of the world's rare earths and other critical minerals, crucial in the manufacture of many high-tech products.

Beijing has already tightened export controls on rare earths as part of previous trade negotiations with the US.

Iran, for its part, has indicated that it wants to establish full control of the Strait of Hormuz - a view that is opposed by the US and most other countries which believe that the passage constitutes international waters and transit should remain unimpeded as it was before the war.

Until recently - and on the basis of the MoU - Iran had been involved in negotiations with Oman, a US ally, to agree a mechanism for administering the strait. However, those talks have so far not produced an agreement and, last week, Trump even threatened to bomb its ally "if it gets in the way" of his administration's own talks with Iran over the issue.

Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi said on Tuesday that he hoped his country and Iran would soon announce the establishment of a temporary shipping corridor in the strait after meeting his Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi in Tehran.

He said in a statement he also hoped for "practical arrangements" to restore safe navigation, adding: "Future management of the strait and a permanent solution will follow in due course."

Araghchi confirmed the meeting in a statement, saying "regional solutions" were discussed in talks with representatives from Pakistan and Oman.

He added that discussions covered the future management of the strait, as well as the framework for a new corridor and a joint mine-clearing operation.

Speaking to state television news after the meeting Iran's Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabad said the entry route to the Gulf would be "through Iranian waters and the exit route through Omani territorial waters, and ships will pass through Iranian waters on both routes".

The minister added that the south corridor of the waterway, which has been recommended to shipping firms by the US and is situated close to the coast of Oman , would be "closed" under the framework, and the meeting "does not mean that the Strait will be opened from tomorrow".

He said "no military vessels will be allowed to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, and only commercial vessels will be allowed to pass through it".

Gharibabad called the route "temporary", adding Iran and Oman will negotiate a new permanent route within a timeframe of 60 days to replace the previous maritime traffic plan.

"If Iran's requests are not granted, the Strait will be closed," he said.

articles.title: Tyler Robinson's lawyers seek camera ban for Sept. 1 hearing, say case is not a 'reality TV show'
articles.summary: Tyler Robinson's attorneys claim cameras and livestreaming of the Sept. 1 hearing risk turning the Charlie Kirk assassination case into a reality TV show.
articles.body: Tyler Robinson's attorneys are again asking the judge to ban cameras from the courtroom, this time alleging that cameras and streaming of his upcoming Sept. 1 hearing risk turning the case into a "reality TV show." "The media presence in the courtroom both distracts and places added pressure on hearing participants to present for the media, as opposed to focusing on the facts, evidence, and mechanics of the hearing," Robinson's attorneys, Kathy Nester, Michael Burt, Richard Novak and Staci Visser, wrote in one of two Saturday court filings. "Mr. Robinson’s case is not and should not be made into a reality TV show." The defense is arguing that livestreams and other images from the hearing could bias the public against their client by showing evidence that may not be admissible at trial later. TYLER ROBINSON RARELY HIT BULLSEYE IN PRACTICE SHOTS, PUTTING BYSTANDERS AT RISK IN KIRK SHOOTING: PROSECUTORS "Specific to the oral argument on the preliminary hearing, the EMC (electronic media coverage) will memorialize and widely disseminate argument discussing the largely hearsay based evidentiary presentation made by the State," the lawyers wrote. "Such evidence is, by its very nature, insufficiently reliable for admission at trial." Read the filings: Both of the filings also included redacted paragraphs after Robinson's lawyers alleged that, "Additional evidence of bias developing as a result of the widespread publication of this case can be tracked in real time." CHARLIE KIRK MURDER CASE AS 'STRAIGHT-FORWARD' AS IT GETS, PROSECUTORS ARGUE AS CASE NEARS TRIAL DECISION The defense also claimed that witnesses who provided statements that were admitted as "reliable hearsay" ahead of the week-long July preliminary hearing "experienced harassment by media and interested third parties." Robinson is the man accused of assassinating Charlie Kirk, 31, at a Turning Point USA event in Orem, Utah, last year. Kirk was shot and killed while speaking to a crowd of thousands at Utah Valley University on Sept. 10, 2025. JUDGE ALLOWS CAMERAS IN CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSINATION CASE, DELAYS PRELIMINARY HEARING Read the filings: Separately, a source close to the Kirk family said Tuesday that Kirk's widow Erika, and his parents, Rob and Kathy, all plan to attend the Sept. 1 hearing together as they did during the July hearing. CHARLIE KIRK MURDER CASE AS 'STRAIGHT-FORWARD' AS IT GETS, PROSECUTORS ARGUE AS CASE NEARS TRIAL DECISION Judge Tony Graf Jr. will hear oral arguments from both sides regarding the evidence introduced in July and will decide whether there's enough probable cause to justify sending Robinson to trial on the charges against him. GOT A TIP? Robinson's defense objected to hearsay evidence from the preliminary hearing and also opposes the sole aggravating factor in the aggravated murder charge that carries the potential death penalty — that Robinson allegedly put other people at great risk of death by shooting Kirk in a crowded place. LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST The defense argued that only a single shot was fired, from an elevated position. It traveled over the crowd, rather than through it, and it only struck Kirk. Prosecutors countered that Robinson was a bad shot, one who "seldom hit the bullseye and sometimes misses the target completely" when practicing shooting with the suspected murder weapon. articles.title: SNAP rolls are shrinking fast. This map shows which states have seen the biggest drops.
articles.summary: Nearly 5.6 million fewer people are receiving food assistance than a year ago, with some states seeing much steeper declines.
articles.body:
The number of people receiving food assistance through the nation's largest federal food aid program has fallen by more than 5 million over the past year.

Participation in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) has decreased by more than 13% as stricter eligibility rules and work requirements take effect. The biggest declines have been seen in the South and Southwest of the country.

Data released by the USDA this month showed SNAP enrollment provisionally fell to 36.6 million in May 2026 from 42.2 million in May 2025. This provisional figure would make the number of people receiving SNAP as low as it was forecast to reach in 2030, according to the Associated Press.

The decline comes as changes to SNAP have expanded work requirements and tightened eligibility rules as part of President Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA).

The changes mean more people must now work, volunteer or take part in job training for at least 80 hours a month to continue receiving SNAP, or risk losing benefits. This rule was extended to include adults up to age 64 and parents of children 14 and older. The law also removed automatic exemptions for veterans, people experiencing homelessness and former foster youth. Exemptions remain for those 65 and older, parents of children younger than 14, and people with disabilities or health limitations.

Some states have seen sharper drops than others, which you can see in the map below.

In Arizona, the number of people receiving SNAP fell by 53.8% from May 2025 to May 2026, while Georgia saw a 36.5% decline over the same period, according to USDA's figures .

Arizona officials said the drop was driven largely by the state's struggles to put the new federal requirements in place.

"Implementing the federally mandated changes triggered unprecedented call volumes and administrative hurdles, including additional verification requirements, creating real barriers for applicants," Brett Bezio, a spokesman for the Arizona Department of Economic Security, told the Associated Press .

Bezio said hiring more staff members and introducing ways for people to submit documents online have helped stem the decline in participation in recent months and reduced the risk that eligible people will lose benefits.

Supporters of the changes introduced by the OBBBA argue that tighter eligibility rules will reduce improper payments and encourage more adults to work.

In an article looking into the fall in SNAP participants last week, the Cato Institute said: "Much of SNAP's enrollment decline reflects states unwinding pandemic-era waivers and eligibility rules that kept caseloads elevated."

It added, "Judge the success of OBBBA's SNAP reforms, and all welfare programs, by how many people move out of welfare and into self-sufficiency, not by how many are kept on it."

Grocery prices in U.S. cities have risen 33% since the beginning of 2019, according to government figures. By comparison, they rose just 6.4% over the previous seven-and-a-half years.

In Florida, where SNAP participation fell 22% in the year to May 2026, Paco Velez, president and CEO of Feeding South Florida, said part of the decline may be driven by immigrants who are in the U.S. legally but fear being targeted by the Trump administration's immigration crackdown if they seek government benefits.

Critics of the SNAP reforms say the new requirements create administrative hurdles that can cause eligible people to lose food assistance.

Some food banks have increased food distributions to try to meet demand that they say has risen as SNAP participation has declined. But advocates say they cannot fully make up the difference.

Reflecting on the changes to SNAP earlier this month, nonprofit No Kid Hungry said: "Already 4.5 million people, including over a million kids, have lost access to SNAP over the past year. Those families are now missing out on the nutritious food SNAP provides, and sadly that number will only grow."

The decline may not be over. Starting in October 2027, states will have to pay a share of SNAP benefit costs if their payment error rates exceed 6% — a change advocates warn could push states to tighten eligibility further to avoid the added expense, potentially creating new barriers for recipients in the years ahead.

articles.title: Lutnick’s last-minute demands derailed Canada trade talks: Reports
articles.summary: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s interventions in the U.S.-Canada trade talks helped the weeks-long negotiations fall apart, according to multiple reports, thrusting the two countries into a trade war. U.S. and Canadian officials had felt good about an outline of a trade deal struck last Tuesday ahead of the original Wednesday deadline. President Trump took to…
articles.body:
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s interventions in the U.S.-Canada trade talks helped the weeks-long negotiations fall apart, according to multiple reports, thrusting the two countries into a trade war .

U.S. and Canadian officials had felt good about an outline of a trade deal struck last Tuesday ahead of the original Wednesday deadline. President Trump took to social media to say that a deal had been struck, and he was pausing the 50 percent tariffs on some Canadian goods until Friday to finalize the paperwork.

But Lutnick was leery of Canadian proposals that would lower the tariff on autos to a level lower than what he wanted, according to The New York Times . He said instead that only a certain volume of aluminum should get lower tariff rates, and that heavy trucks should not have tariffs lowered like cars.

Canada produces some heavy trucks at the General Motors and Ford plants in Ontario.

Canadians put the blame on Lutnick for moving the goalposts at the eleventh hour, according to Bloomberg , while some business leaders were happy he was making demands on a deal they saw as hurting the U.S. metals industries.

When asked Saturday whether Lutnick’s involvement in the final days of negotiations was an impediment, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said that’s “a question for the U.S. administration.”

Carney said his Canadian team was “unified … but you cannot say that about the United States administration.”

The talks between the U.S. and Canada fell apart on Friday, just hours before the tariffs were set to go into effect on items including wine, hockey sticks, cement and others.

Canada vowed to “match those tariffs dollar for dollar.” The tariffs apply to around $20 billion of Canadian goods.

Since then, Trump has threatened further hits on Canada — in the form of 50 percent tariffs on cars, trucks, auto parts and steel that would go into effect on New Year’s Day.

He accused Canada of “ripping off the United States of America for years” in a Truth Social post.

“On Trade, and in other ways, also, they are among the worst Nations in the World to deal with,” he wrote. “They feel entitled, and yet, WE DON’T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED US! They do 95% of their business with the U.S., with us, the exact opposite!”

Canada said Monday it is expected to unveil retaliatory tariffs on the U.S. on Tuesday. They would go into effect on Sept. 8.

articles.title: Indiana power outages: Gov. Braun demands NIPSCO investigation as Gary residents hit day 13
articles.summary: State officials want the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission to investigate how NIPSCO customers’ dollars were spent.
articles.body: After nearly two weeks without power for thousands of people across northwest Indiana, Gov. Mike Braun is calling for an investigation into NIPSCO. “NIPSCO is a monopoly utility that Hoosiers pay every month with the expectation that it will use its considerable resources to maintain its system, prepare for severe weather and restore service as quickly as possible when disaster strikes,” Braun said in a news release. “NIPSCO has failed to keep its end of the bargain.” Braun is calling for a thorough review of NIPSCO’s preparation for and response to the recent power outages. On Monday, he directed the Indiana Office of Utility Consumer Counselor to file a complaint and petition the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission to launch an investigation into NIPSCO. The governor said the crews on the ground did an extraordinary job but “NIPSCO management has failed to deliver adequate solutions.” In response, NIPSCO said it will continue to communicate with Braun’s administration. “NIPSCO values the regulatory process and will cooperate fully if the Commission were to open an investigation. We are committed to transparency and cooperation in providing information regarding our operations and ongoing efforts to serve our customers safely and reliably,” the company said in a statement. There are streets all over the region, including in Hammond, Munster and Gary, where people still don’t have power. Every day, Andre Abrams hopes today will be the day power returns to his neighborhood in Gary. “It’s been a lot of stress,” Abrams said. “It’s Day 13 now. Tomorrow [is Day] 14.” Two weeks without electricity has forced his family to find new ways to get by, including using a lighter to light up the stove in order to cook. “Four workers went to the back to check out the transformer yesterday but ... we need a whole new pole,” said Makinna Cain. The good news is NBC Chicago did see NIPSCO, contracted linemen and ComEd on the ground in Gary. “Without lights, we’re worried about staying here in the dark, but we don’t want to leave our house because somebody might break in it. Then that leaves us with more problems,” said Jamesetta White, who lives in Gary. “I know they’re probably doing the best they can do. I don’t want to put anyone down. I just pray to God that they hurry up.” NIPSCO said it’s “committed to restoring power safely and as quickly as possible for every customer affected by this historic storm.” Families across the area said they’ve had to throw out food. There are health concerns, too. “I have a heart monitor and once the electricity has been off this long, the hospital, the doctors cannot monitor that monitor because it’s off. So, hopefully nothing has happened to me yet,” said Rutha Taylor, who lives in Gary. State officials are asking the commission to investigate how NIPSCO customers’ dollars were spent, including more than $81 million meant for vegetation management from 2023 to 2025 and $2.3 billion meant to replace aging infrastructure since 2016, according to a spokesperson for the Indiana Office of Utility Consumer Counselor. “Since we lost our food and have been out with our lights, I think they should not have us to pay a bill for a whole month. That would give us [time to] catch up,” White said.

articles.title: El coche nuevo más barato de mantener en Estados Unidos es uno que casi nadie compra
articles.summary: El Fiat 500e lidera un estudio como el coche nuevo más barato de mantener en EE. UU., mientras híbridos y eléctricos muestran importantes diferencias en cost...
articles.body:
Comprar un coche y mantenerlo durante años son dos cuestiones muy diferentes. Un estudio de Self.Inc que analiza 50 modelos nuevos vendidos en Estados Unidos ha dejado un resultado tan curioso como inesperado: el Fiat 500e es el coche nuevo más barato de mantener del mercado, con un coste medio anual de apenas 3.557 dólares.

El dato resulta todavía más llamativo si tenemos en cuenta que el pequeño eléctrico italiano prácticamente ha desaparecido de las calles estadounidenses: Fiat vendió solamente 150 unidades durante la primera mitad del año, un 81% menos que en el mismo periodo de 2025.

El Fiat 500e gana gracias a unos costes sorprendentemente bajos

El secreto del Fiat 500e está principalmente en su reducido tamaño, su mecánica eléctrica y unos gastos contenidos en prácticamente todas las categorías analizadas.

Su coste energético anual se sitúa en 779 dólares, exactamente la misma cantidad estimada para el seguro, mientras que el mantenimiento representa otros 1.275 dólares. Los impuestos y tasas suman 724 dólares.

En conjunto, el modelo italiano se distancia claramente del segundo clasificado, el Honda Civic Hybrid , que alcanza 4.833 dólares anuales. Tras ellos aparecen el Hyundai Elantra , con 4.904 dólares; el Nissan Versa , con 4.949; y el Toyota Camry Hybrid , con 5.031 dólares.

La clasificación también deja una conclusión interesante para quienes están pensando en electrificarse. Aunque pueda parecer lógico que un eléctrico sea siempre más económico de mantener, el estudio señala que los vehículos híbridos presentan un coste medio anual de 5.734 dólares, frente a los 6.189 dólares de los eléctricos.

Los coches de gasolina son los más costosos de media, con 7.025 dólares anuales.

Entre los 20 modelos más económicos también aparecen el Honda Accord Hybrid, Honda Civic, MINI Cooper, Kia K4, Mazda3, Dodge Charger Daytona, Tesla Model 3 y Hyundai Ioniq 6, demostrando que existen alternativas muy diferentes para quienes buscan reducir el coste de propiedad.

En el extremo contrario aparece uno de los deportivos más reconocidos del mundo. El Porsche 911 encabeza la lista de los coches nuevos más caros de mantener, con un coste medio anual de nada menos que 10.832 dólares.

El modelo alemán está seguido por el Audi RS7 , con 10.334 dólares; el Cadillac CT5-V Blackwing , con 10.265; el Chevrolet Corvette , con 10.213; y el eléctrico Lucid Air , con 10.049 dólares. En este último caso, el reducido gasto energético no evita que el seguro y otros costes eleven considerablemente la factura anual.

La evolución respecto al estudio anterior también resulta significativa. El gasto medio anual en combustible ha descendido de 2.246 a 1.727 dólares, pero esa mejora ha quedado parcialmente neutralizada por el incremento del seguro, que pasó de 1.763 a 2.219 dólares, y del mantenimiento, que aumentó desde 1.633 hasta 1.817 dólares. Además, los impuestos y tasas también han subido.

Por eso, al comprar un vehículo nuevo no basta con mirar el precio de adquisición o el consumo homologado: seguro, mantenimiento, impuestos y energía pueden cambiar por completo la cuenta final.

Entre los modelos más interesantes por equilibrio aparecen el Nissan Versa, Toyota Camry Hybrid, Honda Accord Hybrid y Mazda3, mientras que incluso propuestas deportivas como el Hyundai Elantra N consiguen sorprender por sus costes relativamente contenidos.

El estudio, eso sí, debe interpretarse como una referencia y no como una garantía de gasto individual, ya que el precio del seguro, los kilómetros recorridos, el estado del vehículo y los costes locales pueden modificar notablemente la factura de cada propietario.

Aun así, el dato del Fiat 500e deja una conclusión difícil de ignorar: el coche que menos cuesta mantener en Estados Unidos es precisamente uno de los que menos éxito comercial está teniendo.

articles.title: Mentmore Towers, Batman Beginsâ Wayne Manor in Buckinghamshire, could be seized as owners face deadline to repair crumbling mansion and conduct bat surveys to save historic property
articles.summary: UK News: The real-life Wayne Manor from Christopher Nolanâs Batman Begins, Mentmore Towers in Buckinghamshire, is at the centre of a preservation battle after .
articles.body: The real-life Wayne Manor from Christopher Nolanâs Batman Begins, Mentmore Towers in Buckinghamshire, is at the centre of a preservation battle after the Grade I-listed mansion was served with a formal repairs notice. The property could ultimately face a compulsory purchase order if its owners fail to take action, while authorities have also required specialist bat surveys before restoration work can proceed.Mentmore Towers, the sprawling country house that doubled as Bruce Wayneâs iconic home in Batman Begins, has been described as being in âvery badâ condition by Historic England. Buckinghamshire Council has now issued a listed-building repairs notice, saying the work is âreasonably necessary for the proper preservationâ of the historic property.The notice comes amid concerns over the deterioration of the mansion, including its roofs, chimneys, rooflights, roof lanterns and leadwork. Photographs included in the notice reportedly show cracks in walls, broken windows and ivy-covered walls. During a visit to the property, officials also found evidence of bats, according to SWNS.Batmanâs Wayne Manor faces a preservation battleMentmore Towers was built between 1852 and 1854 for the Rothschild family and is considered the only major surviving work of architect Sir Joseph Paxton, who also designed Londonâs Crystal Palace.The mansion later gained global pop-culture recognition when it was used as Wayne Manor in Christopher Nolanâs Batman Begins. The property has also appeared in films including The Mummy Returns, Ali G Indahouse and Johnny English.Its cinematic history, however, has not prevented growing concerns about its physical condition.Buckinghamshire Council has ordered the owners to demonstrate that they are appointing a contractor with experience in repairing listed buildings. The authorities have also required three bat-emergence surveys to be completed by August 2027, along with any necessary Natural England licence and recommendations arising from the surveys.Once repair work begins, council and Historic England officers must also be permitted to inspect the property weekly.Council warns of possible compulsory purchaseThe repairs notice represents a significant escalation in the long-running concerns surrounding Mentmore Towers.If the required action is not taken, Buckinghamshire Council could seek government approval to acquire the mansion through a compulsory purchase order, alongside pursuing further legal action.The development has been welcomed by heritage campaigners.Henrietta Billings, director of SAVE Britainâs Heritage, said the organisation welcomed Buckinghamshire Councilâs decision to require the current owner to undertake âurgent and overdue repairsâ to the historic house.âWe urge the owners, who have owned the building for over 25 years, to step up and undertake immediate repairs,â she said. âThis exceptional landmark has been neglected for too long.âWho owns the real Wayne Manor?Mentmore Towers is owned by Syrian-British businessman Simon Halabi, who purchased the property in 1999 after it had been put up for sale two years earlier.Halabi had ambitious plans for the estate, intending to transform Mentmore Towers into a luxury hotel featuring 171 suites.Those plans became embroiled in a legal battle in 2004 after local resident Jonathan Davey obtained a last-minute injunction at the High Court to stop the proposed development.A judicial review subsequently examined whether the conditions attached to the planning permission had been followed. In March 2005, the High Court ruled that the decision to grant planning permission was âunimpeachableâ.However, the proposed luxury hotel never became a reality. Halabiâs property company later ran into financial difficulties amid the collapse of the housing market, and the hotel plans were abandoned.From Rothschild mansion to Batmanâs Wayne ManorBefore Halabi acquired the property, Mentmore Towers had already undergone several changes in its history.In 1992, the previous owners established a country club at the estate, complete with an 18-hole golf course. The club eventually ceased trading in 2015.More recently, company documents filed with Companies House in May reportedly show that Mentmore Towers Ltd, of which Halabi is a director, is a dormant company, meaning it is not currently trading or generating other income such as investments.Despite the uncertainty surrounding its future, Mentmore Towers remains one of Britainâs most recognisable historic estates.Mentmore Towersâ Hollywood historyFor Batman fans, the property is best known as Wayne Manor in Batman Begins, where it provided the exterior setting for Bruce Wayneâs ancestral home.But its screen history extends well beyond Gotham.Mentmore Towers has featured in The Mummy Returns, Ali G Indahouse and Johnny English, while its grand interiors and distinctive architecture have also appeared in music videos.The mansion was used in Haddawayâs âWhat Is Loveâ music video and the Spice Girlsâ âGoodbyeâ video.Now, however, the historic building faces a very real battle far removed from the fictional world of Batman. Unless the necessary repairs, ecological surveys and preservation measures are carried out, the future of the real-life Wayne Manor could ultimately be decided by the authorities.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Canada announces ‘dollar for dollar, rate for rate’ retaliatory tariffs on US
articles.summary: Canada announced retaliatory tariffs on hundreds of American products as high as 50 percent Tuesday, just days after the collapse of negotiations between the two countries. Canadian Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said Canada will match the U.S.’s tariffs “dollar for dollar, rate for rate.” The tariffs would take effect Sept. 8. He said the 15…
articles.body:
Canada announced retaliatory tariffs on hundreds of American products as high as 50 percent Tuesday, just days after the collapse of negotiations between the two countries.

Canadian Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said Canada will match the U.S.’s tariffs “dollar for dollar, rate for rate.” The tariffs would take effect Sept. 8.

He said the 15 percent, 25 percent and 50 percent tariffs will be on $27.6 billion of imports from the U.S.

“For each product, our tariff will match the American tariff on the same type of Canadian good,” he said.

Arguably the biggest measure is Canada doubling its tariffs on U.S. steel and aluminum to 50 percent to match the 50 percent the U.S. put on Canadian steel and aluminum.

“Those tariffs will have real consequences for Canadian workers, businesses, and communities across our nation,” Champagne said of the U.S. tariffs. “Canada must respond, and today we are in a proportionate, targeted, and strategic way.”

He said the countertariffs “are designed primarily to provide protection for Canadian industries impacted by the U.S. tariffs and allow them to compete against U.S. products in the Canadian market.”

Canada released a list of over 700 items that will be targeted with tariffs ranging from live fish, frozen fish, cheese, some apparel, carpets and metal products made of steel or aluminum, among others.

The U.S.’s 50 percent tariffs went into effect on Saturday across over $20 billion of Canadian imports after negotiations collapsed late Friday.

Trump threatened to impose 50 percent tariffs on a plethora of Canadian imports in response to “discriminatory” trade measures. The U.S. tariffs fall under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, the administration said when announcing them last month.

Section 338 is a long-dormant law that allows the president to impose tariffs of up to 50 percent on a country found to discriminate against U.S. products. It does not require an investigation before tariffs are imposed.

Trump on Monday then threatened to hit Canada with 50 percent tariffs on imported cars, trucks, auto parts and steel, which would take effect on New Year’s Day.

“Canada has been ripping off the United States of America for years,” he wrote on Truth Social. “Their ridiculously high tariffs on our Farmers and farm products has made life impossible for these great American Patriots, and has long created a 60 Billion Dollar Deficit between our two Countries. Not sustainable, and NOT ANYMORE!”

Trump said Canada will no longer “be treated like a State.”

“On Trade, and in other ways, also, they are among the worst Nations in the World to deal with,” he said. “They feel entitled, and yet, WE DON’T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED US! They do 95% of their business with the U.S., with us, the exact opposite!”

Canada for its part has remained strong against the U.S. measures. Canadian officials also announced a $7.5 billion CAD package to help support domestic businesses that are harmed by the tariffs.

articles.title: Nevada wildfire contained to 27 percent as thousands still displaced
articles.summary: The third wildfire in two weeks devastates neighbourhoods across Reno, home to major entertainment and casino resorts.
articles.body:
Fire containment has reached 27 percent in the rampant wildfire that first erupted in the Sierra Nevada foothills near the city of Reno in the state of Nevada in the United States. At least seven people – three first responders and four civilians – have been injured.

The blaze first broke out on Saturday and exploded in size by Sunday, destroying at least 32 homes and damaging six as it spread perilously close to dense neighbourhoods. Local officials, speaking at an afternoon news briefing on Monday, said those numbers are sure to rise as assessment teams begin to survey the charred areas.

They also said the fire had no new growth and has held steady at about 60 square kilometres (23 square miles) since it burned out of control on Sunday.

“We are making progress,” assured US Forest Service District Ranger Matt Zumstein.

Videos posted on social media showed the smouldering ruins of homes and cars, with only a scorched basketball hoop still standing.

By Monday, the number of residents under evacuation orders and warnings was lowered to about 63,000, down from more than 90,000 people when the blaze first mushroomed over the weekend. While winds have eased, there are still concerns that gusts could propel the flames through dry brush into newly developed neighbourhoods in Nevada’s largest city outside of metro Las Vegas. Reno is home to about 280,000 people.

Schools across the local area were closed because of the evacuations and to keep roads clear for emergency crews.

‘Like nothing I’ve seen before’: Reno faces third wildfire in two weeks

Reno Mayor Hillary Schieve said the way the fire spread so quickly at its peak had her fearing for the worst.

“It lit up these areas like nothing I’ve seen before,” she said Monday, adding, “it took your breath away, in the worst way”.

This is the third large wildfire in the craggy, high-desert region north of Reno in just the past two weeks – driven completely by human behaviour, according to fire officials. They have not disclosed whether the Hawk Fire, which is what the blaze is known as due to having started near the Hawk Meadow Trail, was intentionally set or accidental. Much of the area that burned was sagebrush and grass.

Resident Crystal Hallock, 53, has lost her home to a fire twice in under a decade. She moved into the rebuilt house in 2019, a year after an electrical fire burned it down.

Nevada’s governor quickly declared a state of emergency in Washoe County over the weekend after mobilising the National Guard to help with aerial firefighting and protecting evacuated neighbourhoods northwest of downtown Reno. But at one roadblock, residents expressed frustration that they could not get back into their homes, according to The Associated Press news agency.

“There’s no fire here! Why are the National Guard here?” a driver yelled.

Washoe County Sheriff Darin Balaam said he understands that some residents are frustrated that they can’t get home, but the danger isn’t over yet. “It just takes that little breeze and one ember,” he said.

Reno is southwest of Nevada’s Black Rock Desert, site of the annual Burning Man festival, which begins on August 30.

Many who travel to Burning Man make Reno a regular pit stop. Organisers on Monday requested that attendees not take hotel rooms and other resources away from fire evacuees, while being mindful of closures.

“Treat our neighbors, first responders, hospitality workers and everyone affected by this emergency with patience and care,” a Burning Man statement read.

Much of Nevada’s western edge is under an increased risk of wildfires this week because of high winds and low relative humidity, the National Interagency Fire Center said. The National Weather Service says the region will see warm, dry and breezy conditions, and that critical fire weather conditions are possible in the week’s latter half. Reno sits at an elevation of 1,370 metres (4,500 feet).

Extremely dry conditions across the American West have sparked a rash of wildfires this summer. Fires in eastern Washington state forced the evacuation of 60,000 people in the Spokane area in early August.

Nationwide wildfires have topped 50,000 this year, marking a 10-year high for the same period, according to the National Interagency Fire Center.

articles.title: Doug Ford responds to Trump’s Lake Ontario taunt: ‘A lot of rhetoric’
articles.summary: Ontario Premier Doug Ford dismissed President Trump’s Tuesday threat to rename a Canadian lake in honor of the U.S., a day after the pair publicly exchanged insults amid an escalating trade fight between the two countries. “I think it’s a lot of rhetoric,” Ford told CNN’s Wolf Blitzer, noting Canada’s role as a “number one…
articles.body:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford dismissed President Trump’s Tuesday threat to rename a Canadian lake in honor of the U.S., a day after the pair publicly exchanged insults amid an escalating trade fight between the two countries.

“I think it’s a lot of rhetoric,” Ford told CNN’s Wolf Blitzer, noting Canada’s role as a “number one customer” for more than a dozen U.S. states.

“We’re strong believers in being a sovereign country, and when President Trump wants to attack our sovereignty and attack our businesses and people in Ontario, I can’t roll over,” he said. “My job is to protect Ontario and Canada, and ironically, protecting the American people.”

The president wrote in a Truth Social post on Tuesday morning that his administration was “giving serious consideration” to renaming Lake Ontario to “Lake America” amid the trade war between the U.S. and Canada.

Trump added that he did not “expect to be doing much business with Ontario any longer.”

The post followed Trump’s earlier move to impose 50 percent tariffs on Canadian goods.

Ford lashed out at these levies on Monday, reiterating his threat to cut the province’s power exports to U.S. states. Ontario’s power grid directly connects to Michigan, New York and Minnesota.

“We power 1.5 million homes and businesses. Everything’s on the table. I’ll do whatever it takes,” the Canadian official told reporters.

Ford called on both sides of the fight to bring down the temperature on Tuesday, acknowledging in his interview with CNN that “things got a little heated” between him and the president.

“Let’s negotiate a fair deal because it’s hurting the U.S. It’s hurting Canada, and we just want to make sure that we have a fair deal,” he said.

Canada announced Tuesday retaliatory tariffs of up to 50 percent on a wide range of U.S. goods that will go into effect on Sept. 8. This came after Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s statement last week that the country would match the U.S. tariffs “dollar for dollar.”

Ford told CNN that the U.S. tariffs ultimately harm Americans.

“I do not understand why he wants to attack Canada nonstop,” he said. “We’re the closest friends and allies, and make no mistake about it, Canadians still love the American people. They love the U.S.”

articles.title: Russia’s infrastructure is being pummeled by Ukrainian strikes. Now Putin wants to seize control of it
articles.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin has signed a decree giving the government powers to temporarily take control of “critical infrastructure” across the country, if private owners fail to protect it from escalating Ukrainian attacks.
articles.body: Russian President Vladimir Putin has signed a decree giving the government powers to temporarily take control of “critical infrastructure” across the country, if private owners fail to protect it from escalating Ukrainian attacks. The new measure comes as Moscow and Kyiv ramp up their air campaigns, with Ukrainian strikes deep into Russian territory sparking fuel shortages and bringing the war closer to home for ordinary Russians. Kyiv has stepped up attacks in recent days on Ozon logistics hubs in Russia – a competitor to the frequently targeted e-commerce giant Wildberries – as it seeks to undermine Moscow’s war-driven economy. The decree, which came into force on Monday, says the new measures are being introduced “in connection with the growing threats to the security of critical infrastructure facilities of the Russian Federation.” It covers a raft of sectors, according to the decree, including fuel and energy infrastructure, communications, transport and logistics facilities, among others. If owners do not take sufficient steps to ensure the “security” of such facilities or restore their functioning quickly enough after attacks, the government can decide to implement “temporary administration,” the decree states. This effectively hands the Russian state control of the owner’s property, property rights and shares. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov on Tuesday said, “quite often the owners of enterprises do not pay proper attention to taking measures to ensure security, anti-drone security.” He also nodded to the support of Western nations for Kyiv as another reason why Moscow “must take measures” to, as he put it, “ensure our own security.” Asked which companies could fall under the remit of the degree, Peskov told reporters the situation would be “analyzed primarily by the government, by the relevant agencies.” “Wherever security measures are not being taken in critical areas, corresponding proposals will be submitted,” he added. Meanwhile, Russia has increasingly been launching high-speed missile attacks across Ukraine, exploiting Kyiv’s shortage of US-made Patriot air defense interceptors, which the country heavily relies upon to shoot down ballistic missiles. It’s a shortage that has been made worse due to a global supply crunch amid the Iran war. Russia launched two missiles and 150 drones at Ukraine overnight into Tuesday, with 124 drones shot down, according to the Ukrainian Air Force. Amid the interceptor shortage, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Kyiv had received a “small number of Patriot missiles,” Ukrainian state media outlet Ukrinform reported Tuesday. “I won’t say which country provided them either – we’ve also received a small number of Patriot missiles. I can’t say how many, but just a few. We need more,” Zelensky said in a meeting with his Estonian counterpart, Ukrinform said.

articles.title: European Court of Human Rights orders Turkey to free Osman Kavala
articles.summary: Philanthropist and activist Osman Kavala has spent almost a decade in jail over charges rights groups say are politically motivated.
articles.body:
The European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) has ordered Turkey to immediately release Osman Kavala, an activist and philanthropist who has been detained in prison for almost a decade.

Kavala was sentenced to life behind bars in 2022 for charges related to nationwide protests in 2013 and a failed coup attempt three years later.

Since his initial arrest and detention in 2017, rights groups and Kavala himself have maintained that the charges against him are politically motivated.

The ECHR on Tuesday ruled that his continued detention was unlawful and that his rights to a fair trial, freedom of expression and association had been violated.

"The measures taken against the applicant... had been predominantly motivated by an ulterior purpose, namely, to punish him for his role in the Gezi Park demonstrations and for expressing his opinions as a human rights defender, and to silence him," the court said in its ruling , external .

The court also found that Kavala's aggravated life sentence amounted to "inhuman and degrading treatment".

Rights advocates and opposition groups say President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's government has increasingly weaponised the judiciary to target critics and rivals.

The court said Kavala's case had exposed a "systemic problem" in Turkey of the "detention and prosecution of political opponents, human rights defenders and journalists", adding that there were "structural shortcomings which affected the guarantees of independence and impartiality of the judiciary".

The Turkish government has insisted the country's courts are independent.

Turkish activist sentenced to life in prison

The case that set Turkey on collision course with the West Published 25 November 2021

The case that set Turkey on collision course with the West

Kavala, 68, became a symbol of a government crackdown on civil society in Turkey following his arrest in October 2017.

He and others were accused of orchestrating and financing anti-government protests in 2013, which started in Istanbul's Gezi park before spreading across Turkey.

The demonstrations posed the first serious challenge to the rule of Erdogan, who was Turkey's dominant prime minister at the time and became its directly elected president the following year.

Human rights group Amnesty International says prosecutors falsely alleged that the Gezi park protests were an attempt to overthrow the government.

In 2019, the ECHR demanded Kavala's immediate release, describing his detention as arbitrary and politically motivated. Turkey did not implement the ruling.

He was initially acquitted in February 2020 but within hours was rearrested on new charges of being part of a failed military coup in 2016.

His acquittal over the Gezi Park protests was overturned in January 2021, and he was sentenced to life in prison in April 2022 - a conviction now declared "null and void" by the ECHR.

Reacting to the latest ECHR ruling, Amnesty International's Eve Geddie said: "This obstruction of justice must end. Turkey's authorities, including judicial and prosecutorial, must act to free Osman Kavala immediately and unconditionally."

Kavala was born in Paris and educated in the UK. Before being thrust to prominence, he ran a cultural centre.

Erdogan has previously accused Kavala of being an agent of the Hungarian-born US billionaire George Soros.

Turkey has refused to comply with the two previous ECHR rulings on Kavala's case, and it is not clear whether Ankara will implement the court's third binding ruling.

The case remains one of the most serious recent flashpoints between Ankara and Strasbourg.

The Council of Europe oversees how its 46 member states execute ECHR rulings. It has the power to freeze a country's membership or suspend its voting rights if it is found to have seriously violated the rule of law.

Even though Turkey has failed to comply with several key ECHR decisions, it remains a founding member, engages with the system and has not broken ties.

A meeting of the Committee of Ministers in mid-September is likely to prioritise the Kavala case, but it remains to be seen whether it will debate harsh punitive measures.

The 33-year-old is accused of attacking the woman while on duty in Swansea city centre in February 2024.

Hall, who resigned from South Wales Police during the IOPC investigation, has also been charged with possession of a firearm and two counts of misconduct in public office.

articles.title: The $20,000 dorm room has arrived. Why Gen Z is taking its home away from home so seriously.
articles.summary: TikTok loves the monograms and custom decor. Students say the real appeal is having a tiny corner of campus that feels like theirs.
articles.body:
For Julie Beth Fox and Kari Cabale, designing the perfect dorms for their newly minted college freshmen was an act of love.

The two stay-at-home moms from Nashville first met when their kids, now in their 20s, were in kindergarten. They became fast friends, going to church together and supporting one another as they raised their combined six children. After years of coming up with fun and easy crafts and designing decor for various high school events, they were eager to flex their creativity to make their kids' rooms perfect, but within reason.

"I wanted her to be confident, and have all the things," Fox tells me of her oldest daughter, who attended Mississippi State. "But I also knew that I was going to set the precedent with her, and if I blew the budget, I would have to continue that. I spent a lot of time thinking it can be elegant, it can be elevated, but it doesn't have to be expensive."

The friends began helping out other moms in their community who found the process of outfitting a dorm room a bit overwhelming, and they loved it so much they decided to start their own company, which they named Petal and Pine Dorm Design . They weren't sure what to expect when they officially launched in June, but the response and the number of clients they have worked with have been beyond their wildest expectations.

"We're kind of overwhelmed and blown away, to be honest," Fox says. "We just thought we'd throw it out there, and we were quite surprised."

Their success is likely due to the fact that dorm design, as a concept, has gone viral. Gone are the days when you'd roll up at your first college living space with an extra-large twin "bed in a box" from Bed, Bath & Beyond and maybe a cute lamp or a poster and call it a day. Now, a perfectly aesthetic, curated dorm can take weeks or even months to create. Some students go all out, spending big bucks to make it perfect.

Beautifully decorated dorms have been trending on social media, particularly TikTok, for a few years, but this year they've hit the cultural zeitgeist in a new way. After a few TikTok videos of elaborately designed dorms being revealed to their gasping undergrads went viral, the internet at large began to obsess over the perfectly curated color schemes, matching monogrammed pillows and, one can assume, hefty price tags for touches like custom built-ins and a shelf to hold their designer bags .

The fascination follows a broader online trend toward a cultural obsession with big public university culture in the South (see: # RushTok ). But the dorm designers I spoke to also believe that the desire for a custom and comfortable room is unique to the current generation of college students. Sure, they want to post beautiful photos to social media to keep up with their peers, but they also value their personal space in a different way.

"Having a beautiful dorm space helps me to feel more at home," Kamryn Hall, a 19-year-old sophomore at Florida State, tells me. When she's not studying, Hall creates content geared toward other college students and has been sharing her journey of designing her second-year dorm room.

"It isn't necessarily about the aesthetics," she says about her choice to invest in her space, which includes a pink ruffled duvet and a custom LED name sign . "It's more about self-expression and getting to showcase everything that I love in a space that's mine and having some feel of individuality, especially when you're in a shared space."

Shannan Bower has worked as an interior designer in Fort Worth, Texas, for 18 years, and added dorm services to her repertoire several years ago. She thinks the fact that Gen Z spent so much time indoors and at home during the pandemic gave them an appreciation of " how your environment can affect the way you feel."

"It's not just about making something pretty for social media," she tells me. "Students want personalization, comfort and a space they can come back to at the end of a long day and genuinely feel at home in. A dorm doesn't have to just be four walls, a bed and a few posters anymore."

Still, for those of us who grew up in that "four walls and a few posters" era, the juxtaposition between what we had and what we see online now can be hilariously stark. Content creator Melanie Ressa, who is 35, jokingly joined the conversation on Instagram by posting a photo of her old dorm, which had one piece of "art": a beer pong poster. She's endlessly fascinated by the rooms she keeps seeing online, she says, because she considers college to be a time when your life should be anything but curated.

"My hot take is that these girls have their entire lives to be adults," she says. "Dorm rooms are not supposed to be perfectly crafted design spaces. What happened to the display of liquor bottle trophies, stolen street signs and posters bought from Spencer's?"

Then there's the debate over costs. After videos of "dorm reveals" from one designer, Shelly Gates of Mississippi, went viral on TikTok last year, she revealed to People that her services can cost up to $20,000 for a custom room. But Fox and Cabale say you don't have to spend a fortune, and most people don't. The extremes may be going viral, but their clients are shopping on Amazon and at HomeGoods (their consultations start at just $100).

Bower advises her clients to invest the most in the items that will be functional for the most important parts of college life: studying and sleeping (what did you think I was going to say?).

"Invest in comfortable bedding and a good mattress topper because sleep is incredibly important for a college student," she says. "Make sure you have functional storage so you're not constantly living in clutter, and create a study space where you can actually spread out and focus."

Fox and Cabale have found that creating a beautiful living space, with the help of parents and/or a decorator, is often a cathartic experience for their young clients. Leaving home and attending college, after all, is a huge life change, and Fox likes to believe that making something cozy and chic can ease jitters for both moms and daughters before they step into the next chapter.

"We feel like it's giving the moms [a chance to] bridge that gap between them being at home and launching them," she says. "It's also giving the girls a lot of confidence and comfort in their new space. … They're really proud of what they're creating."

images.caption: In this era of dorm decor, a ratty duvet and posters just won't do. (Photo illustration: Yahoo News; photos: Shannan Bower Home/Instagram, Petal and Pine Dorm Design)

articles.body: China has warned that it could take retaliatory measures if the United States significantly expands secondary sanctions targeting Chinese companies doing business with Iran, according to reporting by the Financial Times.The warning came after the Trump administration on Monday announced new sanctions targeting companies in Hong Kong and mainland China as part of a broader crackdown on Iran's oil trade. While China's state-owned refiners largely comply with US sanctions on Iranian crude, smaller private refiners, known as "teapots", continue to import and process Iranian oil.The United States has sanctioned some of those refiners this year, but Beijing has instructed Chinese companies not to comply with such measures.The prospect of broader US secondary sanctions comes at a sensitive point in US-China relations. US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are expected to meet in Washington next month, with the leaders expected to discuss extending a one-year truce in their trade dispute.Wang Dong, a senior scholar at Peking University, told FT that Beijing would defend its national interests if Washington moved ahead with broader sanctions, though he said it remained unclear whether the US threat was serious or a negotiating tactic.Zhu Feng, an international relations expert at Nanjing University, told the newspaper that China was also keen to see the conflict between the United States and Iran de-escalate.Zhu said continued restrictions on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz were putting additional pressure on the global economy and could pose a greater risk to China because of its dependence on Middle Eastern oil supplies."From a Chinese perspective, we don't want to get involved in a US-Iranian fight," Zhu told FT.Chinese officials have also stepped up diplomatic contacts in the Middle East. articles.title: Tyrone Noling: Gov. Mike DeWine to decide fate of Ohio death row inmate claiming innocence
articles.summary: Now the fate of the convicted double murderer, whose case has attracted support from Kim Kardashian and other celebrities, is in the hands of Gov. Mike DeWine.
articles.body: The Ohio Parole Board recommended Tuesday that a prisoner who has spent 30 years on death row for two murders he says he did not commit should have his sentence commuted to life in prison with the possibility of parole as early as 2029. The recommendation landed on Gov. Mike DeWine’s desk a week after Tyrone Noling asked the board for a full pardon. Now the fate of the 54-year-old Noling, whose bid for exoneration has garnered celebrity support from Kim Kardashian and actors Hilarie Burton and Jeffrey Dean Morgan, is in the hands of an outgoing Republican governor who, as a state senator, co-sponsored the legislation that reinstated capital punishment in Ohio in 1981. Since then, DeWine has had a change of heart, and in June he called on lawmakers to eliminate the death penalty, saying “the moral justification I had for voting for the death penalty simply no longer exists.” “We are encouraged that the Parole Board has taken a step towards recognizing the gross injustice Tyrone Noling has endured for decades,” said Brian Howe of the Ohio Innocence Project, one of Noling’s attorneys. “We hope Gov. DeWine will pardon Tyrone and allow an innocent man to go home at last.” DeWine has the power to pardon Noling, but he can also reduce his sentence or stay the execution to provide more time to pursue a legal remedy. One of the eight parole board members who took part in this case, former prosecutor Shontell Walker, was in favor of granting Noling a pardon, according to the board’s recommendation. Five were in favor of commuting his sentence and two were opposed. Noling, whose case has been the subject of documentaries and true-crime podcasts, has said he won’t accept a commutation of his sentence to life without parole. Typically, death row inmates aren’t allowed clemency hearings until they have an execution date. Noling doesn’t have one. And during his appearance before the parole board, his lawyers argued that he had nothing to do with the murders of an elderly couple. Prosecutors, however, have insisted that Noling is an unrepentant killer who at age 18 was part of a gang that did a string of robberies in Portage County, where he gunned down Bearnhardt and Cora Hartig, both 81, on April 5, 1990, inside their home in Atwater Township. Bearnhardt Hartig was shot three times and his wife five times with a .25-caliber automatic handgun. Their house had been ransacked. Noling was convicted on the strength of testimony from three other members of the gang who were 14, 15 and 16 at the time. They later retracted their statements, saying that police pressured them to name Noling as the shooter. While aggravated burglary charges brought against Noling were dropped in 1992, a grand jury reindicted him in 1995 for the Hartig murders. Noling was sentenced to death in 1996, even though no physical evidence tied him to the crime and no murder weapon was ever found. While Noling languished on death row, the Innocence Project lawyers uncovered law enforcement notes that pointed to three other potential suspects, including Dan Wilson, who was executed by lethal injection in Ohio in 2009 for the 1991 murder of a young woman. The Ohio Innocence Project lawyers wrote in court documents that the accused man’s original defense team was not aware, during his murder trial, that Wilson’s foster brother had told police that Wilson had bragged about killing the Hartigs. Also, Noling’s defense attorneys were aware that DNA testing on a cigarette butt found by detectives on the Hartigs’ driveway did not place Noling — or any of the three other teens — at the scene at the time. But they weren’t aware of a June 1991 blood-typing lab report that concluded that the cigarette could have been smoked by somebody like Wilson. Noling also got a boost from former Portage County Sheriff Ken Howe, now 83, whose department spent over two years reviewing the case but refused to hand it over to prosecutors because no weapon or physical evidence linked Noling and the other teenagers to the crime. It was the local prosecuting attorney and his investigators who secured the grand jury indictment against Noling. In an interview with The Associated Press, Howe said that there were red flags when police were investigating Noling for the slayings and the evidence that has accumulated since then has convinced him that neither Noling nor the other members of the alleged robbery gang were involved in the double murder. “I believe that these boys were, and are, innocent,” he said.

articles.title: British police arrest 5 more in fatal weekend crash; 17 now charged
articles.summary: British police said they arrested five people in their probe of a crash that killed seven people, bringing the number of people arrested to 17.
articles.body:
Aug. 25 (UPI) -- British authorities said they arrested five people Tuesday in their investigation following a weekend crash that killed seven people, bringing the total number of people arrested to 17.

The new arrestees include three people -- ages 16, 18 and 21 -- facing charges of of participating in an organized crime group; a 55-year-old arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender; and a 23-year-old accused of making threats to kill, The Guardian reported.

The announcement comes one day after police in Cleveland, which serves the Teesside area of northeast England, announced the arrests of 12 people Monday, identifying those detained as nine men and three women between the ages of 19 and 61.

They were detained on a range of offenses, including allegations of participating in organized crime, possession of an offensive weapon and drug-related crimes.

Two of those arrested Monday appeared in court -- Kai Beattie, 19, on a charge of possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life, and Cameron George, 26, charged with drug offenses and possession of criminal property.

The suspects were detained over the weekend in a wide-scale investigation following a collision early Saturday involving a Volkswagen Passat and a police vehicle on the A66, resulting in the deaths of the five occupants of the Passat and two officers in the police vehicle.

Authorities were initially alerted early Saturday to reports of two vehicles being driven dangerously in Middlesbrough. A Volvo XC60 was allegedly seen ramming properties, while a Volkswagen Passat was believed to be associated with the Volvo. Police said both vehicles were operating with cloned license plates.

Police later spotted the Passat and pursued it for nearly 7 minutes before the Passat entered the A66 at South Bank, traveling against traffic, prompting the pursuing police vehicle to end its case.

However, seconds later, at 3:39 a.m., the Passat collided with a second police car, which was traveling in the correct direction, authorities said .

The deceased officers ere identified as Matthew Blades, 37, and Tom Clough, 38. The deceased occupants of the Passat were named as Cole Robert Worthy, 17, Theo Rae, 17, Makai Saddington, 18, and 23-year-olds Jakub Matusiak and Michael Robert Cahill.

"The events of that tragic night will have a lasting and profound impact on the Cleveland area and the communities we seek to protect," Assistant Chief Constable Wayne Fox said Monday in a statement.

The BBC reported Tuesday that the Passat belonged to a man who lived in one of the houses that had been rammed by the Volvo. After the vehicle hit the home, the man's son, Worthy, and five others got into the Passat and drove off.

Fox said they have a duty to investigate the "serious criminal activity" that led to the fatal crash and bring those responsible to justice, though it was not clear how those detained were involved.

"Our robust response will continue in the weeks and months to come, as we continue to tackle those that seek to cause harm to our communities and tackle serious and organized crime," Fox said.

articles.title: China, India hold border talks, agree to continue search for boundary settlement
articles.summary: BEIJING, Aug 25 (Reuters) - China and India agreed on Tuesday to continue dialogue and seek a "fair, reasonable and mutually acceptable settlement" of their...
articles.body:
BEIJING, Aug 25 (Reuters) - China and India agreed on Tuesday to continue dialogue and seek a "fair, reasonable and mutually acceptable settlement" ‌of their border issue after talks between senior diplomats in ‌Beijing.

The world's two most populous nations, both nuclear powers, share a roughly 3,800-km (2,400-mile), largely undemarcated ​and disputed border in the Himalayas.

Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and India's National Security Advisor Ajit Doval had "comprehensive, in-depth, friendly and candid" discussions on border affairs and bilateral ties, China's foreign ministry said in a statement.

Wang said China-India ‌relations were no longer ⁠only of bilateral importance but carried global and strategic significance, saying the two neighbours should strengthen communication and reduce ⁠their differences.

The Indian Embassy in China confirmed in a post on X that the two sides had reviewed bilateral ties and had discussed ways to ​further expand ​cooperation and maintain stability and peace ​in border areas.

Ties between Beijing ‌and New Delhi have gradually improved in recent years following a deadly 2020 border clash, which led to a four-year military standoff before a disengagement agreement was reached in October 2024.

Last year Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi visited China for the first time in seven years, in a sign ‌of a thaw in relations. More recently, ​a fresh border-related dispute triggered sharp diplomatic ​exchanges between the two rivals.

"Both ​sides should learn from historical experience, place the border ‌issue in an appropriate position in ​bilateral relations, and ​move forward without stagnation, regression, or deviation," Wang was quoted as telling Doval at Tuesday's meeting.

The two countries have agreed to hold ​the next round of ‌border talks in India in 2027, the Chinese statement added.

(Reporting by ​Beijing Newsroom, additional reporting by Bipasha Dey in Bengaluru; Editing ​by Alex Richardson and Gareth Jones)

articles.title: Florida voters have approved $35 million to buy and transform 5.8 miles of underused railroad into a trail that will form part of an 11.4-mile greenway and help close a gap in a planned 400-mile trail network
articles.summary: US News: Voters in the coastal Florida city of Bonita Springs have approved a $35 million general obligation bond, clearing the way for the local government to.
articles.body: Voters in the coastal Florida city of Bonita Springs have approved a $35 million general obligation bond, clearing the way for the local government to buy a key 5.8-mile stretch of unused railway. The ballot decision unlocks the missing central section of the wider 11.4-mile Bonita Estero Rail Trail (BERT). The project will also help close an important gap in the planned Florida Gulf Coast Trail, a 400-mile network that is intended to run across Southwest Florida. The referendum was held during the 18 August primary election. It allows the city council to issue up to $35 million in general obligation bonds with a 30-year repayment period. According to public election filings, $28.6 million will be used to buy the 5.8-mile inactive railway corridor from the Fay family, owners of the Seminole Gulf Railway. The rest will pay for engineering, design and the first stage of construction from downtown Bonita Springs.Completing the regional puzzleThe vote removes the final financial hurdle to buying the full 11.4-mile railway corridor, which covers about 180 acres across Southwest Florida. Neighbouring authorities had already committed money to secure their parts of the line. The Village of Estero to the north pledged $19.8 million to buy nearly four miles of track, while Collier County to the south committed $11.6 million for its 1.5-mile section. The combined purchase price agreed by the three jurisdictions is $60 million, about 20 per cent below the property's total appraised value. Because Bonita Springs lies between Estero and Collier County, its approval was seen by conservation groups as the key step needed to secure the entire corridor. "With the positive vote from Bonita Spring residents, we have the final piece in place for the purchase of the rail corridor for BERT," said Deb Orton, President of Friends of BERT, in a statement released through the Trust for Public Land. "Our next step is to complete the due diligence efforts that move us closer to the finalization of the purchase in October. The voters have given the Bonita Springs City Council a clear mandate they sought when they voted to place the referendum on the August 18th ballot for consideration."Cost and local debateThe $35 million bond will be repaid through local property taxes over 30 years. Financial estimates from PFM Financial Advisors show that the measure will add between $49 and $88 a year to the property tax bill for an average home valued at $441,137. Supporters, including the Naples Pathway Coalition, said this works out to about $4.75 a month per household. The project received strong support from local businesses and conservation groups, but there was also opposition before the vote. Some homeowners living next to the unused tracks raised concerns about privacy and security because of increased public access. Others questioned the cost of the project or suggested keeping the corridor available for possible light rail in the future. City leaders, however, argued that turning the abandoned railway into a paved path for walkers and cyclists would provide greater public benefits. They pointed to improved pedestrian safety, better regional connections and potential benefits for local businesses.A wider conservation projectThe Trust for Public Land (TPL), a national non-profit focused on land conservation and public parks, has played a major role in the project. TPL worked with city officials, the Naples Pathway Coalition and Friends of BERT volunteers on the corridor's valuation and public campaign. "Today, Bonita Springs voters made a bold endorsement to invest in a better future for their community," said Doug Hattaway, Southeast Region Conservation Director at Trust for Public Land. "Voters have resoundingly authorized its City Council to fund the corridor's purchase along with significant construction funding of the 5.8-mile Bonita Springs portion of the longer 11.4-mile rails-to-trails project involving also the Village of Estero to the north and Collier County to the south." The completed 11.4-mile trail will give runners, walkers and cyclists a new regional route while also connecting with the planned 75-mile Paradise Coast Trail, which is expected to stretch from Marco Island to South Lee County. The Paradise Coast Trail will then connect with the larger Florida Gulf Coast Trail, a planned 400-mile route linking communities from Naples towards the Tampa Bay area. With voters now approving the bond, city officials and project partners are conducting environmental checks and completing property assessments before the purchase is formally closed. The transaction is expected to be completed in October. Design work for the first paved sections in central Bonita Springs is expected to begin soon after the purchase is finalised.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
