articles.title: Meet Hannah Joseph, the Ohio sophomore who pitched a nonprofit helping seniors use technology and won an AI leadership award
articles.summary: US News: Hannah Joseph, a sophomore at Indian Hill High School in Ohio, has won the 2026 AI Next Generation Award after pitching her nonprofit, Seniors Go Digi.
articles.body: Hannah Joseph, a sophomore at Indian Hill High School in Ohio, has won the 2026 AI Next Generation Award after pitching her nonprofit, Seniors Go Digital, at Cincy AI Week, Village Press reported. She stood out among hundreds of professionals.Since launching in June 2025, Seniors Go Digital has taught hundereds of older adults how to use smartphones, stay safe online and even understand basic AI tools, with help from over 20 student volunteers.Joseph attended Cincy AI Week through Indian Hill Experienceships, a programme that connects students with real-world learning opportunities. The programme operates within the Indian Hill Entrepreneursâ Center. She took part through the school district's partnership with Cincinnati AI Catalyst, which gave her an opportunity to learn alongside professionals working with artificial intelligence.For Joseph, however, the experience was about more than learning about AI. She said her biggest lesson was that a person's age should not stop them from taking initiative.âCincy AI Week was incredibly eye opening. I learned so much about the possibilities of AI, but my biggest takeaway was something entirely different- initiative has no age requirement,â Joseph said.She said she was surrounded by hundreds of professionals during the event. Rather than allowing her age to make her stay quiet, she made an effort to meet people and learn from them.âSurrounded by hundreds of professionals, I chose not to let being the youngest person in the room make me the quietest,â she said.Joseph introduced herself to attendees, asked questions and stayed after sessions to meet speakers. She also used the opportunity to pitch Seniors Go Digital, her nonprofit.Her approach ultimately led to her being considered for the Cincinnati AI Leadership Awards. According to Indian Hill High School's announcement, Joseph became the first teenager ever considered for and honoured with a Cincinnati AI Leadership Award.âIt showed me that being the youngest person in the room does not limit the impact you can make when you are willing to step forward,â Joseph said.Indian Hill High School Principal Andy Gruber praised Joseph for making the most of an opportunity to enter an unfamiliar professional setting.âHannah represents what we hope for every student, the courage to step into an unfamiliar space, the curiosity to learn from the people around her, and the confidence to contribute her own ideas,â Gruber said.âHannah took full advantage of the opportunity, and this recognition speaks volumes about her initiative, leadership, and willingness to make an impact,â he added.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Fortescue defended keeping an executive at work during a harassment investigation; days later it reversed course and suspended the employee
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Fortescue is facing renewed scrutiny over workplace conduct as an external investigation into allegations involving a senior executive runs alongside .
articles.body: Fortescue is facing renewed scrutiny over workplace conduct as an external investigation into allegations involving a senior executive runs alongside separate legal action brought by former employees. The mining company has confirmed that law firm MinterEllison is examining the allegations, while the executive remains employed as the inquiry continues. At the same time, a class action filed in July alleges broader workplace misconduct, including sexual harassment. The case follows similar proceedings involving BHP and Rio Tinto, putting workplace culture across some of Australia's biggest mining companies under growing attention.Fortescue's own annual figures add another layer to the story, with reported psychosocial breaches falling during the latest financial year. But those numbers cover a wider range of workplace concerns and cannot be treated as a direct measure of sexual misconduct. The separate investigations, court cases and internal reporting figures show how difficult it can be to assess workplace conduct through any single set of numbers.Fortescue has hired MinterEllison to investigate allegations against an unnamed senior executiveFortescue confirmed that MinterEllison had been engaged to examine allegations concerning the unnamed senior executive. The company has also sought outside legal and governance advice about how the matter should be handled while the inquiry continues.Gus Pichot, Fortescue's energy chief, said during an earnings call that the company believed it was following the appropriate process. The executive remains employed while the investigation is taking place.That arrangement means the allegations have not yet been resolved. The investigation is intended to establish what happened and whether any workplace rules or standards were breached.The allegations were first reported by the Australian Financial Review earlier in August. Fortescue has not publicly identified the executive involved.98 psychosocial breaches, with 11 dismissals over misconduct recordedThe investigation comes alongside Fortescue's annual disclosure of workplace conduct figures. The miner recorded 98 psychosocial breaches during the latest financial year, a 20% fall from the previous year.The category covers a range of workplace concerns rather than sexual harassment alone. It includes matters such as ethical issues and other incidents that can affect employees' psychological wellbeing.Fortescue said 11 employees had been dismissed for breaches of its code of conduct involving discrimination and sexual harassment. Its internal findings included 13 cases of inappropriate sexual contact, 10 cases of sexual harassment and one case classified as sexual assault.âSexual harassment, unlawful discrimination and any behavior that makes people feel unsafe have no place at Fortescue.âAs reported by Australian Financial Review (AFR), the company employs 16,154 people. Those figures provide a broader picture than the investigation involving the senior executive. They cover cases dealt with across the organisation during the financial year and do not indicate the outcome of the current inquiry.Mining's long-running workplace problemSexual harassment has remained a difficult issue for Australia's resources industry, particularly in Western Australia, where mining is a major employer and workplace culture at remote sites has faced scrutiny for years.A state inquiry into sexual harassment in the resources sector began in 2021. Its findings brought greater attention to complaints about inappropriate behaviour and the difficulties workers can face when reporting misconduct in workplaces where power structures can be pronounced.The issue has not been confined to Fortescue. BHP, the world's largest mining company by market value, reported 380 sexual harassment complaints in its latest financial year, an 11% reduction from the previous year. It also said 109 employees had been dismissed for sexual harassment and 22 for racial harassment.BHP's workforce, including contractors, numbers more than 84,000 globally, so its figures cover a much larger employee base than Fortescue's.Rio Tinto sees Care Hub reports climb, highlighting the limits of comparisonsReportedly, Rio Tinto has reported a different trend in the number of matters reaching its employee support system. The miner recorded 702 incidents through its Care Hub during 2025, a 24% increase from the previous year. The service deals with a broad range of harmful or disrespectful workplace behaviour, including harassment, rather than focusing solely on sexual misconduct.The figures from the three mining companies cannot be read as a direct league table. Their reporting systems, definitions and workforce sizes differ, and an increase in reports can reflect changes in reporting behaviour as well as changes in the underlying level of misconduct.A fall in complaints does not necessarily mean every form of harmful behaviour has declined, just as a rise can sometimes indicate that employees have become more willing or able to report what they experience.Western Australia has seen a fall in reported casesAs reported by Reuters, WorkSafe Western Australia also points to a reduction in incidents reported to the state regulator. WorkSafe recorded 28 incidents involving sexual assault and harassment during the first six months of 2026. That compares with 113 incidents across the whole of 2025 and 421 in 2022.The regulator linked the decline to the work of a specialist team established after the state inquiry. The team has expanded the regulator's capacity to respond to reports involving sexual harassment and assault.The figures cover reports received by the regulator and should not be taken as a measure of every incident occurring across the state's workplaces. Many cases may never reach a regulator.Fortescue faces legal action as its senior executive misconduct probe continuesFortescue is also facing legal action over alleged workplace misconduct. A class action filed in July alleges misconduct including sexual harassment and sex discrimination. The potential damages have not yet been specified.The case was brought by law firm JGA Saddler, which has also filed class actions against BHP and Rio Tinto over alleged workplace misconduct. Those proceedings, launched in late 2024, remain before the courts. The legal cases and Fortescue's internal figures are separate from the investigation now being conducted by MinterEllison. The external inquiry concerns allegations against a particular senior executive, while the class action addresses broader claims about workplace conduct.For Fortescue, the immediate issue is therefore being handled on two fronts: an investigation into allegations involving a senior figure and continuing legal scrutiny over wider workplace practices.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2022, CaseOh was mowing lawns and making TikToks after work; two years later, he won Content Creator of the Year
articles.summary: US Streamers News: Case Dylan Baker, known online as CaseOh, had a pretty normal working life before the internet changed everything for him. He was doing maintenance wo.
articles.body: Case Dylan Baker, known online as CaseOh, had a pretty normal working life before the internet changed everything for him. He was doing maintenance work with his father in rural Arkansas, handling things like plumbing and mowing lawns. Streaming was something he had wanted to do since his early teens, inspired by creators like Nadeshot and the early OpTic Gaming scene. But his first attempts at making videos did not really go anywhere. Then came September 2022. Baker started uploading batches of funny NBA 2K23 clips to TikTok, timing them around the release of new versions of the game. The move worked way faster than expected. Within 48 hours, he had gained more than 10,000 followers, and on September 11, he went live on Twitch for the first time. Just two years later, the same creator was standing at The Game Awards, winning Content Creator of the Year.CaseOhâs first big break came from NBA 2K23 TikToksThe TikTok strategy became the first real turning point. Instead of slowly building an audience, Baker pushed several short, energetic clips around NBA 2K23. The sudden follower growth gave him a reason to move those viewers toward Twitch.His early streams were not exactly running on a perfect setup either. Because of limited internet infrastructure in rural Arkansas, he famously had to use a mobile hotspot for some broadcasts. Still, the growth kept coming. By November 2022, less than two months after starting, he received an invitation to the Twitch Partner Program.His audience helped turn CaseOh into a variety streamerNBA 2K was only the beginning. Baker eventually moved into indie games, simulators, low-budget horror titles and Roblox. Games like Contraband Police and Supermarket Simulator became part of the variety format that defined his streams.A huge part of the appeal was his interaction with chat. Viewers regularly threw food-related jokes at him, including lines like âBuilt like a 1x1 Lego pieceâ and âCase-a-dilla.â His mock-rage reactions and quick ban-hammer moments became a recognizable part of the streams.CaseOh went from Arkansas maintenance work to The Game AwardsOn December 12, 2024, the journey reached its biggest point yet. At The Game Awards at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles, Baker won Content Creator of the Year.He beat a field that included Usada Pekora, Typical Gamer, Techno Gamerz and IlloJuan. He had also picked up multiple Best Variety Streamer awards at The Streamer Awards.For Baker, the win carried a very specific meaning. He had gone from long days of blue-collar maintenance work in a small Arkansas town to one of the biggest creator awards in gaming. His victory speeches repeatedly returned to that background, showing that the entire jump happened while he stayed rooted in the same story: an average guy from Arkansas finding a massive audience by being authentic and consistent.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 200,000 visas could be revoked by the Trump administration. Here's who's affected and what happens next
articles.summary: The State Department is expected to announce the revocation of B-1 and B-2 visas issued over the past decade.
articles.body:
The Trump administration is preparing to revoke up to 200,000 business and tourist visas held by foreign nationals who have applied for or are seeking asylum in the U.S., according to department documents obtained by the Associated Press .

The State Department is reportedly going to announce the action in the coming weeks. If the plans are carried out, it is believed it would represent the largest single mass visa revocation in U.S. history.

"We are coordinating with Department of Homeland Security to identify and revoke the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently," State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott told the Associated Press .

Here's what you need to know about what visas the government is targeting and what happens next.

The State Department is expected to announce in the coming weeks the revocation of B-1 and B-2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026 whose holders have sought asylum.

Foreign nationals apply for a temporary B-1 visa or B-2 visa if they are visiting the U.S. for business or tourism.

Foreign nationals entering the country for business apply for B-1 visas to attend a business convention or conference, settle an estate, negotiate a contract or meet with business associates.

B-2 visas are for people visiting the U.S. on vacation. They would also apply for those seeing friends or relatives, seeking medical treatment, competing in amateur competitions or taking recreational courses that are not university-accredited.

Visa holders are usually let into the country for six months at a time. Border officers have some flexibility to admit someone for longer, up to a year, and if that's still not enough, people can apply to USCIS for a further extension, usually another six months.

Holding a B-1 or B-2 visa doesn't stop someone from applying for asylum. The two are entirely separate immigration processes, and doing one doesn't require or exclude the other.

However, when current applicants apply for a B-1 or B-2 visa, they are asked to confirm that they intend to return to their home country and are not planning to seek asylum, according to AP.

Under federal law , both immigrant and nonimmigrant visas can be revoked by the State Department at any time, including after someone has already traveled to the U.S.

Courts generally can't second-guess that decision, either. There's almost no way to challenge a visa revocation in court. The only exception is if someone is already in deportation proceedings and the revoked visa is the sole reason they're being removed, according to a Congressional Research Service report published in July.

If someone's B-1 or B-2 visa is revoked and they are already living in the U.S., if they leave the country for any reason, even briefly, they likely won't be allowed to re-enter. Their old visa would be void, so they'd have to apply for a new one from abroad, with no guarantee it would be approved.

Canceling someone's visa does not mean they will be immediately deported. Revoking a visa and deporting someone are two separate legal actions, handled by two different government agencies. The State Department can cancel a visa, but it takes a separate decision by the Department of Homeland Security to actually start the deportation process. Until that happens, the person isn't removed.

Someone whose visa is revoked doesn't lose every legal protection. If they're placed in deportation proceedings, they're still entitled to a hearing. That said, unlike in criminal cases, the government won't provide them a lawyer; they'd need to find one themselves or seek free legal aid.

People with pending claims could be recategorized but lose their status as business or tourism travelers, according to the AP report.

The State Department is expected to formally announce the plan in the coming weeks, though nothing is final yet. No policy has been published in the Federal Register, and officials have cautioned that both the scope and the process could still change before it's carried out.

Pigott, the State Department spokesperson, has said the process would be rolling rather than a single announcement: "As the process will be ongoing, the number of revocations remains dynamic and will be done on a rolling basis."

Legal challenges are widely expected. Courts have already pushed back on a related immigration move by the administration: a federal judge recently vacated Secretary of State Marco Rubio's suspension of immigrant visa processing from 75 countries, ruling it exceeded his statutory authority.

The Trump administration has so far revoked about 175,000 visas , the State Department said in August, the majority of which were due to "law enforcement encounters" such as assault, driving under the influence, theft, and drug crimes. Overstays and public criticism of U.S. policy have also been cited as reasons .

A brief timeline of immigration actions since January 2025

Jan. 20, 2025: Trump returns to office and signs an executive order seeking to limit birthright citizenship , launching a broad immigration crackdown.

May 27, 2025: The State Department pauses new student visa interview appointments worldwide for F, M and J visas, as it moves to expand social media vetting.

June 4, 2025: A presidential proclamation bars full or partial entry to the U.S. from 19 countries.

Jan. 12, 2026: The State Department discloses the cumulative visa revocation total has surpassed 100,000 since Trump's inauguration, including about 8,000 student visas.

Jan. 14-21, 2026: The State Department announces a "full review" of screening policies , then pauses immigrant visa issuance for nationals of 75 countries.

Feb. 2, 2026: Plaintiffs sue Secretary of State Rubio over the 75-country visa pause.

June 30, 2026: The Supreme Court affirms birthright citizenship, striking down the president's Jan. 2025 order.

Aug. 6, 2026: Trump signs two executive orders in a new attempt to curtail birthright citizenship, despite June's Supreme Court ruling rejecting his previous effort.

Aug. 10, 2026: The State Department discloses the cumulative total of visas revoked has reached more than 175,000 since Trump's inauguration. This is at a pace of more than 10,000 revocations a month in 2026, up from about 8,000 a month in 2025.

Aug. 21, 2026: A federal judge vacates Rubio's 75-country visa pause , ruling it exceeded his statutory authority.
